Patent Issued for Statement proof and verification (USPTO 12664251) nChain Licensing AG NewsRx.com
2026 JUL 09 (NewsRx) -- By a News Reporter-Staff News Editor at Information Technology Business Daily -- According to news reporting originating from Alexandria, Virginia, by NewsRx journalists, a patent by the inventor Larraia, Enrique (London, GB), filed on March 30, 2023, was published online on June 23, 2026.
The assignee for this patent, patent number 12664251, is nChain Licensing AG (Zug, Switzerland).
Reporters obtained the following quote from the background information supplied by the inventors: “A blockchain refers to a form of distributed data structure, wherein a duplicate copy of the blockchain is maintained at each of a plurality of nodes in a distributed peer-to-peer (P2P) network (referred to below as a “blockchain network”) and widely publicized. The blockchain comprises a chain of blocks of data, wherein each block comprises one or more transactions. Each transaction, other than so-called “coinbase transactions”, points back to a preceding transaction in a sequence which may span one or more blocks going back to one or more coinbase transactions. Coinbase transactions are discussed further below. Transactions that are submitted to the blockchain network are included in new blocks. New blocks are created by a process often referred to as “mining”, which involves each of a plurality of the nodes competing to perform “proof-of-work”, i.e. solving a cryptographic puzzle based on a representation of a defined set of ordered and validated pending transactions waiting to be included in a new block of the blockchain. It should be noted that the blockchain may be pruned at some nodes, and the publication of blocks can be achieved through the publication of mere block headers.
“The transactions in the blockchain may be used for one or more of the following purposes: to convey a digital asset (i.e. a number of digital tokens), to order a set of entries in a virtualised ledger or registry, to receive and process timestamp entries, and/or to time-order index pointers. A blockchain can also be exploited in order to layer additional functionality on top of the blockchain. For example blockchain protocols may allow for storage of additional user data or indexes to data in a transaction. There is no pre-specified limit to the maximum data capacity that can be stored within a single transaction, and therefore increasingly more complex data can be incorporated. For instance this may be used to store an electronic document in the blockchain, or audio or video data.
“Nodes of the blockchain network (which are often referred to as “miners”) perform a distributed transaction registration and verification process, which will be described in more detail later. In summary, during this process a node validates transactions and inserts them into a block template for which they attempt to identify a valid proof-of-work solution. Once a valid solution is found, a new block is propagated to other nodes of the network, thus enabling each node to record the new block on the blockchain. In order to have a transaction recorded in the blockchain, a user (e.g. a blockchain client application) sends the transaction to one of the nodes of the network to be propagated. Nodes which receive the transaction may race to find a proof-of-work solution incorporating the validated transaction into a new block. Each node is configured to enforce the same node protocol, which will include one or more conditions for a transaction to be valid. Invalid transactions will not be propagated nor incorporated into blocks. Assuming the transaction is validated and thereby accepted onto the blockchain, then the transaction (including any user data) will thus remain registered and indexed at each of the nodes in the blockchain network as an immutable public record.
“The node who successfully solved the proof-of-work puzzle to create the latest block is typically rewarded with a new transaction called the “coinbase transaction” which distributes an amount of the digital asset, i.e. a number of tokens. The detection and rejection of invalid transactions is enforced by the actions of competing nodes who act as agents of the network and are incentivised to report and block malfeasance. The widespread publication of information allows users to continuously audit the performance of nodes. The publication of the mere block headers allows participants to ensure the ongoing integrity of the blockchain.
“In an “output-based” model (sometimes referred to as a UTXO-based model), the data structure of a given transaction comprises one or more inputs and one or more outputs. Any spendable output comprises an element specifying an amount of the digital asset that is derivable from the proceeding sequence of transactions. The spendable output is sometimes referred to as a UTXO (“unspent transaction output”). The output may further comprise a locking script specifying a condition for the future redemption of the output. A locking script is a predicate defining the conditions necessary to validate and transfer digital tokens or assets. Each input of a transaction (other than a coinbase transaction) comprises a pointer (i.e. a reference) to such an output in a preceding transaction, and may further comprise an unlocking script for unlocking the locking script of the pointed-to output. So consider a pair of transactions, call them a first and a second transaction (or “target” transaction). The first transaction comprises at least one output specifying an amount of the digital asset, and comprising a locking script defining one or more conditions of unlocking the output. The second, target transaction comprises at least one input, comprising a pointer to the output of the first transaction, and an unlocking script for unlocking the output of the first transaction.
“In such a model, when the second, target transaction is sent to the blockchain network to be propagated and recorded in the blockchain, one of the criteria for validity applied at each node will be that the unlocking script meets all of the one or more conditions defined in the locking script of the first transaction. Another will be that the output of the first transaction has not already been redeemed by another, earlier valid transaction. Any node that finds the target transaction invalid according to any of these conditions will not propagate it (as a valid transaction, but possibly to register an invalid transaction) nor include it in a new block to be recorded in the blockchain.
“An alternative type of transaction model is an account-based model. In this case each transaction does not define the amount to be transferred by referring back to the UTXO of a preceding transaction in a sequence of past transactions, but rather by reference to an absolute account balance. The current state of all accounts is stored by the nodes separate to the blockchain and is updated constantly.
“Blockchains provided a decentralised and permission-less global mechanism that enables a solution to the problem of fair-exchange between two mutually un-trusting parties without the need for third party arbitration or escrow. The fair exchange of data or information, for financial reward or in exchange for information such as digital goods, is embodied in a transaction protocol known as a Zero-Knowledge Contingent Payments (ZKCP). In a ZKCP, specified data is transferred from seller to buyer only if a payment is confirmed, and the payment from buyer to seller is only completed if the specified data is valid according to the conditions of the sale. Details of such a protocol are known but it is essentially based on the combination of a hash-time-locked contract (HTLC) with a zero-knowledge proof, which simultaneously verifies that some encrypted information (the ‘digital good’) is valid/correct and that the ‘password’ to decrypt this information is the data that must be revealed on the blockchain to claim the payment.
“The central component of a ZKCP protocol is a zero-knowledge proof for a series of dependent statements about data/information validity or correctness, key validity and its corresponding hash value. Such complex composite statements require an efficient zero-knowledge proof system for general computations: in essence, this enables one party to run an arbitrary program with secret inputs and then prove to another party that the program accepted the inputs as valid and was executed correctly-without revealing anything about the secret inputs or the execution of the program.
“Zero knowledge SNARKs (zkSNARKs) provide a method of proving, in zero-knowledge, the validity of arbitrary computations that can be expressed as arithmetic circuits. The two main distinguishing properties of zkSNARKs are that they are non-interactive (the prover sends the proof to the verifier in one move) and succinct (the proof is small and easy to verify).”
In addition to obtaining background information on this patent, NewsRx editors also obtained the inventor’s summary information for this patent: “Known Zero-knowledge Succinct Non-interactive ARguments of Knowledge (zk-SNARKs) are an implementation of a general purpose proof system for arithmetic circuit satisfiability. In the SNARK framework, a statement encoded as an arithmetic circuit is converted into a construct called a Quadratic Arithmetic Program (QAP), which consists of a set of polynomial equations. The statement can them be proved by demonstrating the validity of this set of equations at a single point. The main advantage of the SNARK method is that the verifier only needs to perform a few elliptic curve (pairing) operations (taking a few ms) and the proof is very small (288 bytes) and independent of the circuit size.
“The very small proof and verification time achieved by the SNARK method comes at the expense of a trusted set-up, non-standard cryptographic assumptions and a much heavier computational burden placed upon the prover. The SNARK method also requires the use of elliptic curve bi-linear pairings. However, the use of computationally feasible bi-linear pairings requires the use of special ‘pairing-friendly’ elliptic curves. This precludes the use of many standard cryptographic elliptic curve parameter sets, including the Bitcoin secp256k1. Statements involving general elliptic curve point-multiplications must then employ explicit circuits (which may be very large).
“Additionally incorporating an explicit elliptic curve multiplication (key-statement) into the circuit, would multiply both the proving key size and proof generation time by at least an order of magnitude.
“The invention enables the zero-knowledge proof of statements that involve elliptic curve public-private key relationships simultaneously with general arithmetic circuit satisfiability. This is achieved with negligible computational expense beyond proving satisfiability of the arithmetic circuit, and avoids the requirement of creating explicit arithmetic circuits for elliptic curve point multiplication operations, which would increase the computational expense of the proof substantially.
“According to one aspect disclosed herein, there is provided a computer implemented method of providing proof that a statement is true while keeping a secret input to the statement a secret, the method performed on a computing device and comprising:”
The claims supplied by the inventors are:
“1. A computer implemented method of providing proof that a statement is true while keeping a secret input to the statement a secret, the method performed on a computing device and comprising: generating a zero knowledge proof using a public input, the secret input, and a proving key linked to an augmented verification circuit, wherein the augmented verification circuit comprises (i) a verification circuit arranged to receive the public input and secret input, supply the secret input to a function circuit representing the statement to generate a function circuit output, and determine whether the public input corresponds to the function circuit output; and (ii) a multiplicative gate arranged to receive the secret input and a dummy value; and wherein the zero knowledge proof comprises a batched commitment to inputs of multiplicative gates of the augmented verification circuit, the batched commitment generated using a first vector comprising n components from a finite group of data elements, wherein each of the n components of the first vector correspond to a respective input of the multiplicative gates of the augmented verification circuit and one of the n components of the first vector is at a position which corresponds to an input wire of the dummy multiplicative gate which is arranged to receive the secret input, and wherein the secret input is a discrete logarithm of a public element of said finite group of data elements; and transmitting the zero knowledge proof to a verifying computing device to enable the verifying computing device to verify that the computing device has knowledge of the secret input.
“2. The computer implemented method of claim 1, wherein the batched commitment is a batched Pedersen commitment.
“3. The computer implemented method of claim 1, wherein the finite group of data elements are of an elliptic curve.
“4. The computer implemented method of claim 3, wherein the public element of said finite group of data elements is a public key and the secret input is a signing key.
“5. The computer implemented method of claim 1, wherein the method further comprises proving that the secret input is the discrete logarithm of the public element.
“6. The computer implemented method of claim 5, wherein proving that the secret input is the discrete logarithm of the public element comprises: generating a further batched commitment, and transmitting the further batched commitment to the verifying computing device; receiving a random challenge from the verifying computing device; generating a response to the random challenge, and transmitting the response to the verifying computing device to prove that the secret input is the discrete logarithm of the public element.
“7. The computer implemented method of claim 6, wherein the further batched commitment is a batched Pedersen commitment.
“8. The computer implemented method of claim 6, wherein generating the further batched commitment comprises: generating a second vector comprising n components, wherein a component of the second vector at a predetermined position, corresponding to the position in the first vector, is set to zero; and generating the further batched commitment by committing to the second vector.
“9. The computer implemented method of claim 8, wherein remaining components of the second vector are random values.
“10. The computer implemented method of claim 8, wherein the finite group of data elements are of an elliptic curve, and generating the further batched commitment to the second vector uses a commitment key vector comprising n components from the finite group of data elements and one of the n components of the commitment key vector is a base point of the elliptic curve at a predetermined position which corresponds to the position in the first vector, the public element obtained by multiplying said base point with the secret input.
“11. The computer implemented method of claim 8, wherein in response to receiving the random challenge, the method comprises: modifying the first vector by replacing the secret input at said position with a zero to generate a modified first vector; wherein the response comprises a response vector generated by combining the modified first vector with the second vector using the random challenge; and transmitting the response to the verifying computing device.
“12. The computer implemented method of claim 11, wherein the method further comprises combining a random element used to generate the batched commitment with a further random element of the further batched commitment to generate a combined random element, wherein the response comprises the combined random element.
“13. The computer implemented method of claim 1, wherein the method comprises transmitting the statement to the verifying computing device.
“14. A computer implemented method of verifying that a statement is true without knowledge of a secret input to the statement, the method performed on a computing device and comprising: receiving a zero knowledge proof from a proving computing device; obtaining the statement; verifying that the zero knowledge proof is valid using the zero knowledge proof, a public input and a verification key linked to an augmented verification circuit, wherein the augmented verification circuit comprises (i) a verification circuit arranged to receive the public input and secret input, supply the secret input to a function circuit representing the statement to generate a function circuit output, and determine whether the public input corresponds to the function circuit output; and (ii) a multiplicative gate arranged to receive the secret input and a dummy value; and wherein the zero knowledge proof comprises a batched commitment to inputs of multiplicative gates of the augmented verification circuit, the batched commitment generated using a first vector comprising n components from a finite group of data elements, wherein each of the n components of the first vector correspond to a respective input of the multiplicative gates of the augmented verification circuit and one of the n components of the first vector is at a position which corresponds to an input wire of the dummy multiplicative gate which is arranged to receive the secret input, and wherein the secret input is a discrete logarithm of a public element of said finite group of data elements; and determining that the proving computing device has knowledge of the secret input based on said verifying.
“15. The computer implemented method of claim 1, wherein an output of the multiplicative gate is not linked to the verification circuit.
“16. The computer implemented method of claim 1, wherein the function circuit implements a hash function and, preferably, an SHA-256 hash function.
“17. A non-transitory computer readable storage medium comprising computer readable instructions that, when read by a computing device, cause the computing device to perform a method of providing proof that a statement is true while keeping a secret input to the statement a secret, the method performed on a computing device and comprising: generating a zero knowledge proof using a public input, the secret input, and a proving key linked to an augmented verification circuit, wherein the augmented verification circuit comprises (i) a verification circuit arranged to receive the public input and secret input, supply the secret input to a function circuit representing the statement to generate a function circuit output, and determine whether the public input corresponds to the function circuit output; and (ii) a multiplicative gate arranged to receive the secret input and a dummy value; and wherein the zero knowledge proof comprises a batched commitment to inputs of multiplicative gates of the augmented verification circuit, the batched commitment generated using a first vector comprising n components from a finite group of data elements, wherein each of the n components of the first vector correspond to a respective input of the multiplicative gates of the augmented verification circuit and one of the n components of the first vector is at a position which corresponds to an input wire of the dummy multiplicative gate which is arranged to receive the secret input, and wherein the secret input is a discrete logarithm of a public element of said finite group of data elements; and transmitting the zero knowledge proof to a verifying computing device to enable the verifying computing device to verify that the computing device has knowledge of the secret input.”

Michael Saylor Selling Isn't Bitcoin's Biggest Problem—Here's What JPMorgan Says the Real Threat Is Parshwa Turakhiya Benzinga
Strategy Inc.’s (NASDAQ:MSTR) Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) sales create periodic selling pressure but are not the main structural threat to Bitcoin, according to a JP Morgan note published on Thursday.
The Real Threat Is Banks Building Their Own Blockchains
Analysts led by managing director Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou argued the bigger danger comes from financial institutions adopting blockchain technology in ways that bypass public networks entirely.
If tokenization, payments, and settlement move to permissioned infrastructure controlled by banks rather than public chains, the broader crypto ecosystem faces slower activity, lower liquidity, and weaker capital flows over time.
“The more important risk stems from blockchain adoption within traditional finance continuing to develop in ways that bypass public permissionless networks,” the analysts wrote.
Why Institutions Keep Choosing Private Blockchains
JPMorgan said institutional adoption has consistently favored permissioned blockchains because they offer better privacy controls, KYC compliance, clearer governance, and greater regulatory certainty.
The Bank for International Settlements has explicitly warned against using public blockchains for systemically important financial infrastructure, instead promoting permissioned ledgers that combine tokenized central bank money with commercial bank deposits.
Banks are already building their own blockchain infrastructure through tokenized deposits, which are digital versions of regular bank deposits backed by existing regulation.
If these become widely adopted, they reduce the need for stablecoins in institutional payments.
SWIFT’s blockchain initiative and central bank digital currency projects like the digital euro and digital yuan would strengthen that trend further.
Real World Assets May Never Move To Public Chains
The tokenized RWA market sits at around $50 billion, with a meaningful share hosted on Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH).
JPMorgan said that likely reflects early experimentation rather than the long-term structure.
As institutional adoption grows, issuance, custody, and settlement could increasingly move to private infrastructure. Public blockchains may still handle distribution but become less central to how institutions actually process transactions.
DTCC is already developing tokenization workflows on permissioned infrastructure while only selectively connecting to public networks.
“Permissioned networks anchor the regulated system and public chains are merely used for distribution and connectivity,” the analysts said.
Even The CLARITY Act May Not Fix This
The analysts noted that even if the CLARITY Act passes this year, it may not eliminate these risks.
Regulatory clarity could accelerate bank-issued tokenized deposits, strengthening incumbents while limiting the role of public blockchain stablecoins.
Three scenarios could challenge JPMorgan’s view: a hybrid model where both blockchain types play meaningful roles, stronger stablecoin adoption from favorable regulation, or Bitcoin continuing to trade as digital gold regardless of how value accrues across the broader ecosystem.

headline: AI Agents Need Their Own Court: Internet Court Uses AI Juries, No Humans Required
detail_text:
AI Agents Need Their Own Court: Internet Court Uses AI Juries, No Humans Required
Matched:
COIN
|Also matched:
IBM
MSFT
Source: Tech Times
Publication Date: 7/12/2026 2:50:16 PM
AI agent dispute resolution reached a milestone July 10 when GenLayer Foundation led 27 firms in launching Internet Court, a protocol where 1,001 AI validators resolve agentic commerce disputes in under an hour for under two dollars per case, no human arbitrator required, just weeks after the AAA launched a competing open standard.
AI Agents Need Their Own Court: Internet Court Uses AI Juries, No Humans Required ACI Information Group
Genlayer.com
AI agents are already negotiating contracts, committing funds, and executing payments with one another — entirely without human sign-off. When one of them fails to deliver, no court on earth can keep up. On July 10, a 27-firm consortium led by the GenLayer Foundation launched Internet Court, the first deployed commercial system in which disputes between autonomous agents are resolved not by a human arbitrator, a human judge, or a human jury, but by a rotating pool of 1,001 AI validators that reach a binding verdict in minutes. No human sits at the bench. That is not an omission — it is the design.
The launch arrived at an inflection point that 65% of enterprises running AI agents have already lived through: at least one agent-related incident in the past twelve months, according to a Cloud Security Alliance survey from April 2026, with more than a third of those incidents producing direct financial losses. The scale of the underlying commerce is larger still — McKinsey projects that AI agents could mediate between $3 trillion and $5 trillion in global consumer commerce by 2030 — and the dispute resolution infrastructure for that economy has been, until now, essentially nonexistent.
AI Agent Commerce Already Has a Dispute Problem — and the Evidence Is Specific
The absence of dispute infrastructure is not theoretical. In January 2026, attackers who had compromised executive devices at Step Finance — a Solana-based DeFi portfolio manager — discovered that the company's AI trading agents held permissions to execute large token transfers without human approval. The agents did exactly what they were designed to do. By the time the breach was discovered, they had moved more than 261,000 SOL tokens, worth roughly $27 million to $30 million at the time, and only $4.7 million was recovered in the Step Finance breach in January 2026. The native token crashed 97%. The company shut down.
That incident involved a security compromise, not a contract dispute. But it illustrates the structural gap at the center of agentic commerce: AI agents hold real authority over real money, operate faster than human oversight can follow, and exist in a legal environment that has no specialized mechanism for resolving what goes wrong at that speed. Disputes on agent-initiated transactions are already running at roughly 2.4 times the rate of comparable human-initiated card-not-present transactions, according to TrustSphere's 2026 agentic-commerce analysis, with a significantly different composition — fewer fraud disputes and more "did not authorize" and "not as described" claims.
Traditional courts operate on timescales of days, weeks, or months. AI agents can execute thousands of transactions per minute. The value of individual disputes may be small, but the volume means the gap between execution speed and resolution speed is a genuine infrastructure crisis, not a future problem.
What Internet Court Built: AI Juries Running on Condorcet's Math
At the heart of Internet Court is GenLayer's Optimistic Democracy consensus mechanism. When a dispute is submitted, a randomly selected subset of AI validators — each running a different large language model — independently reason through the submitted evidence. One validator is designated as the leader and proposes a verdict. The remaining validators commit their votes without seeing each other's positions, then reveal whether they agree. If consensus is reached, a 30-minute challenge window opens; any party can contest the result by posting a bond, at which point the jury expands — from an initial group of five validators to eleven, and further as needed — until finality is reached.
The design is grounded in Condorcet's Jury Theorem, formulated by the French Enlightenment mathematician Nicolas de Condorcet in 1785: under certain assumptions, the probability of a group reaching the correct answer increases as the number of independent evaluators grows. GenLayer uses a validator pool of 1,001, drawn from across a diverse set of open-source AI models, to reduce the risk that any single model's biases or failure modes dominate the outcome.
The validators run inside GenLayer's GenVM — a sandboxed execution environment — and evaluate disputes through Intelligent Contracts, a GenLayer-native extension of smart contracts written in Python. Unlike traditional smart contracts, which execute rigid, predetermined logic based on deterministic on-chain data and cannot evaluate ambiguous situations, Intelligent Contracts can process natural language, fetch live web data, and assess context and nuance. "Partial performance" and "disputed quality" — the two situations that conventional smart-contract logic handles worst — are exactly the cases the system is designed for.
Resolution costs, per GenLayer's published benchmarks, run from roughly $0.85 to $1.45 per case, with a typical resolution time of 30 to 60 minutes. That price is achievable because enforcement does not require off-chain machinery: verdicts bind the escrow already locked in the smart contract at the outset of the transaction. A winning ruling releases funds; a losing ruling redirects them. No bailiff, no sheriff, no collection process.
This system has been live in testnet form since June 2025 (Testnet Asimov) and in a second testnet phase in 2026 (Testnet Bradbury). As of the consortium's launch, GenLayer's network dashboard showed the network processing roughly 350,000 transactions per day, or approximately 20,000 to 25,000 decisions. "Internet Court is the shared place agents can turn to when a deal goes wrong," said David Riudor, CEO and co-founder of the GenLayer Foundation. "Machine-speed money needs machine-speed adjudication."
What the Consortium Brings and Why the Stack Fragmentation Matters
Internet Court's founding coalition of 27 firms is a signal about the actual problem the protocol is trying to solve, which is not only dispute resolution but interoperability. Agentic commerce currently runs on a collection of siloed standards: Coinbase's x402 handles micropayments (now open-sourced to the Linux Foundation, with AWS, Google, Microsoft, Stripe, and Visa as supporting members); Ethereum's ERC-8004 manages agent identity; Google's A2A handles agent-to-agent interoperability. Each standard solves one layer of the stack and leaves the rest for agents to negotiate independently.
"Internet Court makes them work together," said Albert Castellana, co-founder and CEO of GenLayer Labs. "With our founding members, we're turning a fragmented space into a single open skill that any agent can use to make financial commitments hold up, even when they're contested."
MetaMask's integration illustrates what "work together" means technically. GenLayer has incorporated the MetaMask Smart Accounts Kit — including ERC-7710 delegations and MetaMask's x402 Facilitator — to enable AI agents to securely authorize blockchain transactions, delegate financial authority within defined scopes, and interact with the dispute resolution system across different platforms. ERC-7710 is a delegation standard that allows an agent to authorize sub-delegations, giving developers precise control over what authority an agent can extend to other agents in a chain of instructions. "AI agents are becoming a core part of how commerce works," said Ryan McPeck, Smart Accounts Lead at MetaMask. "MetaMask is building at the frontier to put them at the center, transacting securely and acting within safe, well-defined permissions."
OKX, for its part, has named GenLayer as the dispute resolution provider for its AI agent marketplace — launched in beta alongside the consortium announcement — making that marketplace the protocol's first large-scale real-world production test. The protocol has also been released as an open-source project on GitHub, with more than 69 reusable components contributed by 23 of the founding organizations.
AI Judges With No Human in the Room: A First in Dispute Resolution History
Online dispute resolution has been studied and practiced since the late 1990s. What it has never done, until now, is remove the human neutral entirely.
In the scholarly framework developed by Ethan Katsh and Janet Rifkin — the foundational theorists of what they called Online Dispute Resolution — technology plays the role of a "fourth party": an independent input to the management of a dispute, distinct from the two disputants and their neutral third party. The technology assists or augments the human neutral. It does not replace the human neutral. Katsh and Wing, in 2006, predicted that virtual "fourth party" avatars would eventually be created to judge disputes and could become more skilled over time. Internet Court is the first commercial deployment that actually instantiates that prediction — not by assisting a human arbitrator but by eliminating the role entirely.
This is not merely a technical distinction. Online dispute resolution scholarship consistently identifies procedural justice — the sense among disputants that the process was fair, transparent, and accountable — as the primary determinant of whether a dispute resolution mechanism earns sustained adoption. Human arbitrators, whatever their limitations, carry a credential that AI validators do not: accountability to professional standards, bar associations, arbitral institutions, and, ultimately, to legal enforcement. When an AI validator pool produces a result that a losing party considers wrong, there is no professional body to complain to, no case number that unlocks a state enforcement mechanism, and no recourse except challenging the result within the same AI-governed system.
Lindsay Lin, former counsel and current COO at New York-based crypto venture firm Dragonfly, articulated the correlation risk that the multi-model design is meant to mitigate: "A lot of LLMs can be correlated because they share training data and common failure modes, whereas humans tend to be more independent," she said, as reported by Forbes. Andrew Hall, a professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business and a research advisor to Andreessen Horowitz's crypto team, has written that AI judges could help scale prediction markets and cannot be bribed — but also cautions that models hallucinate and can be manipulated through clever prompts or corrupted training data.
GenLayer argues that using different model families across the validator set reduces the risk of correlated failure. Whether the diversity of 1,001 validators is sufficient to overcome shared training-data biases is a question the OKX beta will begin to answer.
Internet Court Is Not Running Unopposed
On June 24, 2026, the American Arbitration Association announced the Legal Context Protocol, a competing standard for agent-to-agent commerce, roughly two weeks before Internet Court's launch. The Legal Context Protocol is co-stewarded with Denver-based blockchain firm Integra Ledger and launched with contributors including Google, IBM, Circle, and Ava Labs.
The architecture is fundamentally different from Internet Court's. Rather than replacing human arbiters with AI validators, the Legal Context Protocol attaches a cryptographic fingerprint to the terms of each transaction, creating an auditable record that a party, court, regulator, or reviewer can later use to verify whether the record matches the agreed terms. The protocol does not require blockchain, but blockchain systems can build on it. It links agentic commerce back to the existing legal system rather than creating a parallel one.
The two approaches represent a genuine fork in how the industry will structure trust in agentic transactions. Internet Court bets that AI validators running at machine speed are adequate arbiters for the volume of low-value disputes that agentic commerce will generate. The Legal Context Protocol bets that the path to legitimacy runs through evidentiary infrastructure that a traditional court can ultimately recognize. Both standards launched in the same two-week window. Both are competing for the same developer mindshare.
Open Questions That the OKX Beta Will Begin to Answer
No serious observer of Internet Court's architecture treats its success as guaranteed, and the open questions are specific.
Legal standing. Internet Court currently has no recognition in any jurisdiction. A verdict binding an escrow contract does not automatically compel any off-chain action. For disputes involving off-chain deliverables — physical goods, partially delivered services, creative work where payment has already been made — the protocol functions as a first line of recourse only. For anything beyond the funds already escrowed, a traditional legal process remains the enforcement backstop. Albert Castellana framed this as the intended scope, not a limitation: "We're not trying to compete with the legal system. We just want to provide an alternative where hiring a lawyer to dispute a claim for $10,000 is not economical. Instead, you can use this system to arrive at a resolution, which may ultimately cost you a few cents."
Adversarial resilience. A system that relies on staking mechanisms and slashing conditions to enforce validator behavior creates new attack surfaces. Coordinated Sybil attacks against the validator pool — in which one actor registers many validator identities to influence outcomes — remain a meaningful risk. So does prompt injection against GenVM's AI models, which a sophisticated actor could use to manipulate verdict proposals. Coordinated false evidence submission is also a credible threat. These are not hypothetical — they are among the documented attack vectors against agentic AI systems generally. The question is whether Internet Court's multi-model validator design and bond-posting challenge mechanism are sufficient defenses. Testnet data provides some signal; the OKX marketplace will provide production-scale stress.
Enterprise adoption ceiling. Enterprises operating in regulated environments — financial services, healthcare, insurance — are unlikely to integrate a non-state arbitration layer without clearer liability frameworks. The European AI Liability Directive, which EU member states must implement by December 9, 2026, explicitly treats AI-enabled software as a "product" for strict liability purposes, creating compliance questions that Internet Court does not yet answer. The CFPB's January 2026 advisory on Regulation Z and agent-initiated transactions establishes that consumer recourse rights are not extinguished by an agent mandate — meaning that even a resolved Internet Court dispute may still be subject to chargeback claims for U.S. consumer transactions.
What Comes Next
The immediate metrics to watch are not headlines — they are numbers coming out of the OKX beta marketplace: dispute volume, average resolution time, verdict consistency across cases with similar fact patterns, and the presence or absence of exploits in the validator pool.
Beyond OKX, the consortium's trajectory depends on adoption outside the founding group. The open-source GitHub library — 69+ reusable components from 23 of the 27 founding firms — lowers the integration barrier, but the Web3 builder community has already seen many open standards that never achieved critical mass. GenLayer plans to expand the validator pool through a public token launch later in 2026, a design choice that aligns validator incentives with protocol health but also introduces the token dynamics that have historically complicated neutral governance in blockchain projects.
What the July 10 launch unambiguously establishes is that the industry's leading Web3 infrastructure firms believe two things simultaneously: that agentic commerce is not a future use case but a present one, and that the gap between transaction speed and dispute resolution speed is large enough to require a dedicated infrastructure layer that looks nothing like any arbitration institution that has existed before. Whether Internet Court or the AAA's Legal Context Protocol — or a third standard not yet announced — becomes the layer that commerce actually trusts is still an open question. The infrastructure race to answer it has now formally begun.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is Internet Court, and how does it work?
Internet Court is a dispute resolution protocol for AI agents — software that can negotiate contracts, commit funds, and complete commercial transactions without human oversight. When two agents disagree over whether a contract was fulfilled, Internet Court routes the dispute to a pool of 1,001 AI validators, each running a different language model. A randomly selected subset evaluates the evidence, a leader proposes a verdict, and the others vote independently. If consensus is reached, the verdict binds the smart-contract escrow attached to the transaction — releasing or redirecting the locked funds without requiring human intervention. The full process typically concludes in 30 to 60 minutes at a cost of roughly $0.85 to $1.45 per case.
Is Internet Court legally binding?
Not in any jurisdiction as of its July 10, 2026 launch. Internet Court's rulings bind only the funds already held in smart-contract escrow before the dispute. For disputes involving off-chain deliverables — physical goods, services, creative work — a verdict can redirect escrowed funds but cannot compel any party to perform any real-world action or pay money held outside the escrow. Traditional legal recourse remains the enforcement mechanism for anything beyond those pre-locked funds. The American Arbitration Association's competing Legal Context Protocol is designed to link agentic commerce to the existing legal system through cryptographic term records rather than replacing that system with AI validators.
What happens when AI agents make financial decisions that go wrong?
AI agent commerce disputes are already happening at meaningful scale: agent-initiated transactions are generating disputes at roughly 2.4 times the rate of comparable human-initiated card-not-present transactions, per TrustSphere's 2026 analysis. In the most extreme documented case, AI trading agents at Step Finance moved roughly $27 million in cryptocurrency without human authorization after attackers compromised executive devices — and only $4.7 million was recovered. The CFPB has clarified in a January 2026 advisory that consumer recourse rights under Regulation Z are not extinguished when an agent makes an unauthorized transaction; the right narrows but does not disappear. For disputes on blockchain-based platforms, Internet Court is one emerging option; traditional chargeback and arbitration mechanisms remain available depending on the payment method used.
Can AI validators be manipulated or biased in ways that corrupt verdicts?
This is the core technical risk that GenLayer's multi-model validator design is intended to address. Lindsay Lin, COO at crypto venture firm Dragonfly, has noted that different large language models can be correlated in their failure modes because they share training data. Stanford professor Andrew Hall, a research advisor to a16z's crypto team, has written that AI judges cannot be bribed — a genuine advantage over human arbitrators in high-volume, low-value dispute contexts — but can be manipulated through prompt injection or corrupted training data. GenLayer's use of a rotating pool of 1,001 validators running diverse open-source models is designed to reduce correlated failure risk. Whether that design holds under adversarial conditions at production scale is the open question that the OKX beta marketplace is now beginning to test.

AscendEX shutdown leaves users without guaranteed fund recovery after the crypto exchange ceased operations July 1, 2026, citing the EU MiCA regulation it never obtained authorization under and a failed liquidity deal. On-chain data showed depleted reserves weeks before closure, while the exchange warned that frozen crypto withdrawals may never be processed.
AscendEX Froze Withdrawals and May Not Return User Funds After MiCA Miss ACI Information Group
Ascendex.com
Crypto exchange AscendEX shut down on July 1, 2026, and as of this writing has given users no timeline and no assurance that their funds will be returned — a situation that on-chain data suggests was visible on the blockchain weeks before the exchange acknowledged any problem. The exchange's failure to obtain authorization under the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation left its users outside the legal protection framework MiCA was specifically designed to provide, creating a painful gap between the regulation's consumer-protection promises and the reality facing the people who most needed them. AscendEX's official closure notice details the terms of the wind-down.
Shutdown Came After Weeks of On-Chain Warning Signs
Blockchain investigator ZachXBT sounded the first public alarm on June 26, 2026, after receiving multiple user reports of withdrawals stuck in an "initiating" state for days or weeks with no transaction hash ever generated. Reviewing AscendEX's known hot wallet addresses using Arkham Intelligence and TRM Labs, he found that the exchange's publicly identifiable operational wallets held almost no major liquid assets — specifically ETH, USDT, USDC, and SOL — the cryptocurrencies users were most likely trying to withdraw. ZachXBT's public liquidity warning was carried in full by Protos and other outlets that cover on-chain investigations.
The on-chain methodology ZachXBT used relies on a core feature of blockchain transparency: publicly labeled hot wallet addresses — the online accounts exchanges use for day-to-day withdrawal flows — can be tracked in real time. The important caveat, which ZachXBT's own framing acknowledged, is that hot wallets represent only the operational slice of a well-run exchange's holdings; the majority typically sits in offline cold storage that may not be publicly labeled. Low hot wallet balances are therefore a yellow flag for liquidity stress, not automatic proof of insolvency. What made AscendEX's situation different was what the broader reserve data showed.
The on-chain records reviewed by Protos showed AscendEX's total reserve balance dropped by more than $240 million on June 20, 2026 — six days before ZachXBT's first warning. That drop followed a liquidity injection of roughly the same size less than two months earlier, before which reserves had held steady at around $50 million. The $240 million injection arrived and left within weeks. By July 8, Arkham Intelligence showed the AscendEX-labeled address held approximately $13.45 million in crypto assets — with more than $12 million concentrated in the exchange's own ASD token and Unbound Science's UNITE token, neither of which carries the liquidity needed to fund user withdrawals at scale.
Exchange Cited Failed Liquidity Deal Alongside MiCA
AscendEX's July 6 notice — sent to users five days after the platform had already shut down — named three reasons for the closure: the absence of authorization under MiCA, which took full effect on July 1; a failed strategic transaction in which a counterparty was supposed to provide platform liquidity but did not perform; and "wider crypto market conditions." The five-day gap between shutdown and notification was not explained.
The exchange's language in the notice was unusually direct about its financial position. It acknowledged that it had depended on the unnamed counterparty's capital, that the capital did not arrive, and that the exchange was "currently assessing the company's financial position and considering what options, if any, may be available in relation to account holders." That conditional phrasing — "what options, if any" — is not language that signals confidence.
Starting July 6, all automated withdrawals were suspended. Every request now goes through a manual review process that includes account verification, KYC/AML/CFT screening, fraud prevention checks, asset and balance reconciliation, network availability confirmation, and any applicable legal or insolvency-related constraints. The exchange stated explicitly that it could not guarantee either the timing or the final amount of funds returned. No account holder was said to be receiving priority over any other.
Users who had been watching carefully got earlier warning than most. One user told Bitpush that their withdrawals were restricted starting May 6 — nearly two months before the official shutdown. AscendEX told that user to cease public activities, notified them on June 12 of a phased settlement process, then authorized a first settlement withdrawal on June 24 that was later reversed with no transaction ID. The total unresolved balance in that single case: 34,174 USDT and 25,592 XRP.
ZachXBT subsequently verified that unresolved user withdrawal claims he had reviewed exceeded multiple seven figures. On July 6 — the same day as the official notice — he published AscendEX co-founder George Cao's personal phone number directly to users who had been unable to reach the exchange. By that date, AscendEX's X account had been silent for two weeks.
MiCA's Protection Guarantee Reaches Exactly the Users Who Least Need It
MiCA's Article 70 mandates that all authorized Crypto-Asset Service Providers — known as CASPs — maintain client funds completely separate from corporate capital. If a licensed platform becomes insolvent, user assets are legally protected from corporate creditors and cannot be liquidated to cover the platform's own debts. It is one of MiCA's central consumer-protection provisions, designed to prevent exactly the scenario now unfolding at AscendEX.
AscendEX never obtained that authorization. The exchange did not hold a CASP license under MiCA, which means Article 70's segregation requirement never applied to it, and its users have no statutory right to the protection it provides. The regulation's consumer safeguard cannot reach the consumers who are suffering the harm it was designed to prevent — because those consumers are on a platform that failed the regulatory test.
Roshan Dharia, CEO of distressed-investment firm Echo Base, explained the economic logic of that failure: the compliance cost of obtaining a MiCA license — estimated at €500,000 to €2 million in the first year, plus ongoing annual costs of €250,000 or more — made authorization economically unviable for a meaningful share of the market's existing operators. Of the estimated 1,100 to 3,000 firms that previously held national crypto registrations across the EU, only around 244 cleared the CASP authorization bar by the July 1 deadline. The rest either chose not to apply, failed to complete the process, or — like AscendEX — made bets on other paths that did not materialize.
Whether This Is a MiCA Story Depends on When the Clock Started
The picture that emerges from AscendEX's collapse is more complicated than a simple regulatory casualty. MiCA provided the proximate trigger — an authorization deadline that forced the question — but the liquidity problem that the on-chain data shows was already present in June, before the deadline. The $240 million that was injected and then withdrawn from AscendEX's reserves did not vanish because of MiCA. It vanished because a strategic transaction failed and because whatever replaced that capital — the stable $50 million in reserves that held for months before the injection — was already insufficient to absorb the withdrawal demand when the exchange shut down.
What MiCA did was make the failure public and unavoidable. Without the July 1 deadline, it is plausible that AscendEX could have continued delaying withdrawals and accepting deposits for considerably longer, in the pattern ZachXBT documented on July 2. The regulation forced a wind-down instead. Whether that wind-down is orderly — ESMA's stated requirement for unlicensed platforms exiting the market — is the live question that AscendEX has not answered.
ESMA itself moved swiftly. On July 8, the authority launched a Common Supervisory Action across licensed crypto firms specifically focused on custody resilience, with national regulators conducting risk-based inspections from late 2026 into early 2027. ESMA did not formally connect the action to AscendEX's collapse, but the timing placed AscendEX's frozen withdrawals before European regulators as the most visible live example of what custody failure costs users. The supervisory sweep covers only authorized CASPs — AscendEX falls outside its scope entirely.
AscendEX Was Not a Fringe Platform
The weight of this collapse is heavier because of what AscendEX once represented. The exchange launched in 2018 as BitMax, founded by George Cao — who holds a PhD in computer science from the University of Chicago — and Ariel Ling. It rebranded as AscendEX in March 2021. At its peak it ranked among the top-ten centralized crypto exchanges globally by trading volume.
In 2021, it raised $50 million in a Series B led by Polychain Capital and Hack VC — institutional validators that placed AscendEX alongside a small number of credentialed, funded platforms in the space. Later that same year, in December 2021, the exchange lost approximately $78 million in a hot wallet hack that blockchain security firms attributed to the Lazarus Group, the North Korean state-sponsored operation responsible for billions of dollars in crypto exchange attacks. AscendEX pledged full reimbursement to affected users then. Its current notice contains no equivalent assurance.
That contrast matters. A platform that once promised full recovery from an external attack — and was backed by institutional capital to make it credible — is now unable to guarantee the return of user funds from an internal failure of its own liquidity management.
What Users With Frozen Withdrawals Should Do Now
Users with assets frozen on AscendEX face a constrained set of options. The practical steps that apply now:
Document everything immediately: Save all account balances, transaction histories, withdrawal requests, and any correspondence with AscendEX support. This documentation will matter if formal insolvency proceedings are opened, as the mechanism for settling user claims will likely be determined by that process.
Submit a withdrawal request through the official platform flow — not through any third party. AscendEX confirmed that all requests go through the same documented review process regardless of who submits them.
Report to financial regulators and law enforcement in your jurisdiction. ZachXBT explicitly urged this step and repeated it on July 8. In the EU, the relevant regulators are the national competent authorities designated under MiCA in each member state; in other jurisdictions, the relevant bodies vary. The reports create a documented record that supports any future insolvency claim process.
Do not engage with any third-party service offering to recover frozen funds for an upfront fee. Recovery scammers specifically target users of distressed exchanges with promises of expedited fund access in exchange for payments that are never returned. These services are uniformly fraudulent. Affected users should report such contact to the same regulators they are already filing reports with.
Direct all correspondence to support@ascendex.com and retain records of every communication.
What Comes Next for AscendEX — and for the Market
Whether AscendEX enters formal insolvency proceedings remains unannounced as of July 12, 2026. The exchange's July 6 notice warned that if such proceedings begin, the treatment of unresolved balances will be determined by the applicable insolvency procedure rather than the current withdrawal-review process — adding another layer of uncertainty for users who are already without a timeline.
For the broader EU crypto market, the MiCA shakeout is still running. Only 244 firms held full CASP authorization at the transition deadline, representing roughly 17 to 24 percent of the field that existed before MiCA. The European Commission is already gathering stakeholder feedback through September 30, 2026 on whether to expand MiCA's scope to cover tokenized securities and non-EU stablecoin issuers — two areas the original framework left outside its reach. The next version of the regulation may close gaps that the current one left open. The users stuck on AscendEX right now cannot wait for that revision.
The lesson that AscendEX's collapse makes unavoidable is one the crypto industry has re-learned repeatedly: custody on a centralized exchange is exposure to that exchange's solvency, governance, and judgment. MiCA's Article 70 is designed to limit that exposure for users on authorized platforms. For everyone else, the protection the regulation promises is exactly the protection they cannot have.
Frequently Asked Questions
Will AscendEX users get their money back?
AscendEX has explicitly stated that it cannot guarantee the timing or the amount of funds returned to users. All withdrawal requests are under manual review with no stated end date. If the exchange enters formal insolvency proceedings — which the July 6 notice warned was possible — user claims will be processed within that insolvency framework, which may mean partial recovery at best. On-chain data as of July 8 showed approximately $13.45 million in AscendEX-labeled reserves, most of which consists of the exchange's own illiquid native tokens rather than the major assets users are likely trying to withdraw.
Why doesn't MiCA protect AscendEX users?
MiCA's core consumer-protection mechanism for exchange users is Article 70, which requires all authorized Crypto-Asset Service Providers to keep client funds legally segregated from corporate capital. That segregation gives users a protected claim in insolvency. AscendEX never obtained MiCA authorization, which means Article 70 never applied to it. The regulation's protection attaches to the license — users on unlicensed platforms have no statutory right to it regardless of how MiCA was marketed as a user-protection framework.
How did on-chain investigators detect the problem before the shutdown?
Blockchain investigator ZachXBT used publicly available tools — Arkham Intelligence and TRM Labs — to examine wallet addresses labeled as AscendEX's known hot wallets. Because all transactions on public blockchains are permanently recorded and pseudonymously visible, hot wallet balances can be tracked in real time. When those balances showed near-zero holdings of major assets like ETH, USDT, and SOL, ZachXBT flagged it as a liquidity warning. The method has inherent limits — cold storage wallets used for the bulk of an exchange's holdings may not be publicly labeled — but the separate on-chain data showing a $240 million reserve collapse on June 20 strengthened the case significantly.
Which EU crypto exchanges are currently MiCA-authorized?
As of the July 1, 2026 deadline, approximately 244 firms held full CASP authorization across EU and EEA member states. Major licensed exchanges include Coinbase (licensed through Luxembourg), Kraken (Central Bank of Ireland), and OKX (Malta). Users who want to verify whether their exchange holds authorization can consult ESMA's official MiCA register, which is published as CSV files on ESMA's official website and updated weekly.

'If You Want to Get Rich Hold Bitcoin,' Prominent Investor Says: 'You Just Didn't Do the Obvious Thing' Parshwa Turakhiya Benzinga
Holding Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) through every downturn is the only strategy that has consistently worked in crypto, according to Dragonfly Managing Partner Haseeb Qureshi.
Yet, he says most people don’t do “the obvious thing.”
The Only Strategy That Has Ever Worked In Crypto Is Holding
Speaking on the When Shift Happens podcast in July, Qureshi said he entered the industry in late 2017 and watched Bitcoin fall from $19,000 to $4,000 with Ethereum dropping below $100.
He said 2018 may have been worse than post-FTX because at least after FTX, investors had someone to blame. In 2018, there was nobody to point a finger at.
“There are so many people I know who came into crypto at the same time I did and didn’t make money,” Qureshi said.
Bitcoin is a bet on something that may become like gold, not something that already is. If the market believes Bitcoin reaches saturation in 10 years, it prices accordingly.
If expectations shift to 15 years, the asset gets marked down sharply even if the terminal value stays the same. His rough saturation price range: well above $100,000, probably below $1 million.
Ethereum And Solana Are In A Growth Regime, Not A Revenue Regime
Qureshi said critics applying a cash flow framework to Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) are using the wrong lens.
Ethereum barely moves when fees increase. It moves on growth expectations, the same way Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) trades on robotics and autonomous vehicle potential rather than current earnings.
AI Eating Crypto Talent Is Actually Healthy
Qureshi said pioneers who need chaos should go find it in AI. Crypto is now in the buildout phase, executing on proven infrastructure.
Social media went 20 to 30x between 2010 and today without a single major new idea after 2010.
Crypto is entering the same phase, and the gains ahead don’t require the Wild West to come back.

“The answer is very simple. You just didn’t do the obvious thing, which is stay in the market.” He said venture capital works partly because it forces investors to hold, with LPs locked up and unable to sell even when they want to.
Institutions Are Still Barely In, And That’s Where The Upside Lives
Most of Dragonfly’s institutional LPs hold less than 1% of their portfolios in crypto. Morgan Stanley only recently started recommending digital assets to high-net-worth clients, and Vanguard just approved BlackRock’s IBIT (NASDAQ:IBIT).
The biggest predictor of who voted for the FIT 21 crypto bill in the House was age, not party. Younger Congress members voted yes, older ones voted no, and Qureshi said crypto adoption follows the same generational curve the cloud shift followed.
Bitcoin Is Not Digital Gold Yet, And That’s Exactly Why It’s Still Volatile
Qureshi pushed back on critics who complain Bitcoin isn’t trading like gold during macro stress.

What explains Bitcoin's price plunge after hitting an all-time high on the market? ContentEngine
Bitcoin lost approximately half its value in less than nine months. After hitting an all-time high of nearly US$126,200 on October 6, 2025, it is currently trading below US$60,000. In the face of such a sharp decline, explanations ranging from geopolitical to almost metaphysical are appearing in forums, TV shows, and research reports. In today's Pocket Finance, we'll try to cut through the noise to distinguish between two aspects that are often conflated: on the one hand, theories that attempt to explain the decline based on specific events (technological risks, regulatory delays, capital rotation) and, on the other, the cyclical pattern that the asset has been exhibiting for more than a decade and which, if it plays out again, would have very specific implications for when this downtrend might end.
Circulating Theories
The first theory to gain traction this year is that of quantum computing risk. In March 2026, a study by Google Quantum AI substantially reduced the amount of theoretical resources needed to break the elliptic curve cryptography that protects Bitcoin's private keys (the difference from previous estimates was on the order of twenty times).
A few weeks later, Jefferies strategist Christopher Wood removed a 10% allocation to Bitcoin from his "Greed & Fear" portfolio model and reallocated it to physical gold and mining stocks, explicitly citing the quantum threat. The consulting firm Bernstein and Ark Invest tempered the alarmism (they estimate it will take between three and five years--and up to ten or fifteen, depending on the scenario--before a quantum computer capable of breaking the encryption exists), but they agreed on something troubling for Bitcoin holders: around 6 to 7 million bitcoins sit in addresses with public keys that have already been exposed, particularly in older wallets, and migrating that stock to secure systems requires protocol updates and social coordination within the ecosystem--two things that don't happen quickly in Bitcoin.
The second theory points to the regulatory front. The Clarity Act (the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, passed by the House of Representatives on July 17, 2025) has been stalled in the U.S. Senate for months. It was not until June 1, 2026, that it was formally added to the Senate's legislative calendar, after months of disputes over three contentious issues (the ban on stablecoins paying yields, ethical rules that would restrict officials with crypto interests, and the scope of protections for software developers).
Senator Cynthia Lummis warned in June that if the bill is not passed in 2026, it may not be considered again until 2030, and firms like Galaxy Digital estimate the chances of passage at around 50% (prediction markets are somewhat more optimistic, ranging from 59% to 72%). The market had priced in regulatory clarity that would unlock long-delayed institutional investments; every week without progress acts as a silent withdrawal of that premium, and the negative outflows in spot Bitcoin ETFs observed since May reinforce this interpretation.
The third theory is probably the most structural and the least discussed in the mainstream media: Bitcoin mining companies are abandoning mining to transition into artificial intelligence data centers. Companies such as Core Scientific, IREN, Hut 8, TeraWulf, Riot, and MARA have signed contracts to provide AI computing power worth more than US$70,000 million over the past twelve months (Hut 8 even signed a 15-year lease in December 2025 worth US$7,000 million with Fluidstack in Louisiana). The reason is purely economic: the average total cost of producing one bitcoin stood at around US$74,300 (CoinDesk, based on industry data), exceeding the spot price for much of the second quarter, while AI contracts offer fixed long-term rates and significantly higher margins. To finance this pivot, several mining companies sold part of their bitcoin holdings (Core Scientific sold nearly US$ 175 million worth in March), and this, combined with the decline in the global hashrate (5.8% in the second quarter, according to KuCoin), led to persistent selling pressure and raised fundamental questions about the network's security.
Repeating Patterns
While theories dominate the headlines, Bitcoin has been exhibiting a pattern since its third halving that has now repeated itself three times. The sharp rally begins approximately one year before the halving (the event that cuts the issuance of new bitcoins in half every four years), continues to hit successive all-time highs until about one year after the halving, and then enters a deep correction. The magnitude of that correction was 85% between 2013 and 2015 (from about $1,127 to $172), 83% between 2017 and 2018 (from 19,666 to around 3,250), and 77% between 2021 and 2022 (from 69,000 to 15,500 following the FTX collapse). The simple average is around 82%, but there is a clear downward trend: with each cycle, the asset's maturation and the influx of institutional capital reduce the percentage decline. A scenario in the range of 70% for this cycle would be consistent with that progression.
In addition to this consistency in magnitude, there is also a temporal pattern. In the three previous cycles, the bear market bottom occurred approximately one year after the all-time high, followed by a sideways consolidation phase lasting about six months, until a new bullish acceleration began one year before the next halving. [La Nación/GDA]
"Pizza Day," the Initial Transaction, and the Losses
On May 22, 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz, a programmer craving pizza, decided to spend 10,000 Bitcoins to buy himself two pizzas. Back then, Bitcoin was a technological novelty with little value, but today, at a value of $57,000 per BTC, those two pizzas would cost a staggering $570 million. This transaction became such a famous milestone that every year, cryptocurrency enthusiasts celebrate "Bitcoin Pizza Day," reminding us that what seems like a trivial whim today could be worth a fortune tomorrow.
On the other hand, the first transaction in Bitcoin's history took place in January 2009, when Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin's enigmatic creator, sent 50 BTC to Hal Finney, a renowned cryptographer and one of the first to believe in the potential of this new technology. At that time, those 50 BTC had no real market value. However, if we look at their value today, we're talking about US$2.85 million. This modest transfer marked the beginning of what would become a global financial revolution, proving that even great ideas start with small steps.
It is also estimated that around 20% of all existing Bitcoins are lost forever due to forgotten passwords, damaged devices, or inaccessible wallets. This means that more than four million BTC can never be recovered, effectively reducing the total supply of the cryptocurrency. This phenomenon underscores the importance of learning how to securely store your Bitcoin holdings.

This movement shows that the quantum risk premium is real, but also that it is subject to the same macroeconomic fluctuations as any other asset.

Coinbase has intensified its defense of the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act, arguing that the proposed legislation would strengthen, not undermine, the United States’ national security framework. The exchange’s response comes after Senator Elizabeth Warren warned that the bill could create new avenues for sanctions evasion and weaken oversight of the crypto industry.
In a statement published on X, Coinbase Chief Policy Officer Faryar Shirzad said the absence of clear digital asset regulations poses a far greater risk than the legislation itself.
He said the bill would strengthen the Treasury Department’s ability to detect and block sanctions evasion, expand resources available to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), and give crypto platforms clearer authority to freeze suspicious transactions when requested by law enforcement.
Rather than creating a regulatory loophole, Shirzad maintained that the legislation would bring crypto firms into a more transparent supervisory framework.
“The argument that the CLARITY Act compromises national security gets it exactly backward.”
He wrote, adding that bad actors benefit most when regulatory expectations remain unclear.
The latest comments were made in response to criticism from Senator Elizabeth Warren, who has repeatedly argued that the current version of the CLARITY Act could weaken U.S. sanctions enforcement.
Earlier this month, Warren described the proposal as a potential “ticket to sanctions evasion,” expressing concerns that parts of the legislation could create compliance gaps that hostile governments, cybercriminal organizations, or illicit financial networks might exploit.
Her objections reflect broader concerns among some lawmakers that the U.S. should prioritize strict financial controls as digital assets become increasingly integrated into the global financial system.
Debate Intensifies Ahead of Key Congressional Decisions
The dispute comes as Congress continues debating several major cryptocurrency bills that could reshape oversight of the industry.
Supporters of the CLARITY Act argue the legislation establishes clear jurisdictional boundaries between the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), while introducing comprehensive compliance standards for digital asset intermediaries.
The bill has gained backing from several industry organizations that believe regulatory clarity would encourage innovation while strengthening consumer protections and enforcement capabilities.
Senator Cynthia Lummis has also defended the proposal, rejecting claims that it would weaken financial safeguards. She recently stated that the legislation contains multiple provisions designed to combat illicit finance, including anti-money laundering requirements, sanctions enforcement measures, and reporting obligations for digital asset firms.
Lummis has warned that failure to advance comprehensive crypto legislation during the current congressional session could leave the United States without a clear regulatory framework for several more years.
The discussion surrounding the CLARITY Act reflects a broader debate over how the United States should regulate the rapidly expanding digital asset sector.
