How Wealth Management Technology Works: A Guide for the US Financial Market ACI Information Group
Start with data. A modern platform first aggregates a client’s accounts, holdings, and transactions, often by connecting to banks and custodians through application programming interfaces. That raw data feeds a planning layer that models cash flow, retirement timing, and tax exposure. Above that sits the portfolio engine, which compares current holdings against a target allocation and decides what to buy or sell. Finally, an execution and reporting layer places the trades, records them for compliance, and renders the result on the client’s dashboard.
None of these layers is new on its own. What changed is that they now connect through software rather than through a person retyping figures from one screen into another. Grand View Research reports that the cloud segment holds the largest share of the wealth management software market and is growing fastest, precisely because cloud platforms let these layers exchange data in real time instead of in overnight batches.
The role of model portfolios and automated rebalancing
The heart of the automation is the model portfolio. An advisor or investment committee defines a target mix, for example 60 percent equities and 40 percent bonds, broken into specific funds. The software then watches every account mapped to that model. When markets push the equity share to 64 percent, the rebalancing engine sells the excess and buys the underweight assets to return to target. It does this across thousands of accounts at once, a task that would take a human team weeks.
The reason this matters is discipline. Left to their own devices, investors tend to let winners run and losers linger, which slowly pulls a portfolio away from its intended risk level. Automated rebalancing removes that drift without emotion. It also removes the temptation to time the market, since the rules fire on preset thresholds rather than on a hunch about where stocks are headed next.
Tax handling rides on the same engine. Many US platforms run tax-loss harvesting, selling a position at a loss to offset gains elsewhere, then buying a similar asset to keep the allocation intact. Done by hand, this is tedious and error-prone. Done by software, it runs daily. The global wealth management software market reached USD 6.28 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow at a 14.7 percent compound annual rate through 2033, per Grand View Research, and rebalancing and tax tools are a large part of why firms keep buying.
Where humans still sit in the loop
Automation handles the mechanical work, but the US market has not removed the human. Grand View Research found that human advisory still led the market with a 57.1 percent revenue share in 2025, because clients want a person for the decisions that do not fit a model: selling a company, planning an estate, or talking through a market crash. The dominant design is hybrid. The software watches the portfolio and surfaces alerts; the advisor decides which alerts deserve a phone call.
That triage is the quiet engine of the business. A platform might flag a client who is holding too much cash, approaching a required minimum distribution, or drifting from a stated goal. The advisor reviews the flags each morning and reaches out where a conversation adds value. The client experiences attentive service; the firm delivers it without doubling its staff.
This division of labor is what makes the technology scale. An advisor who once managed 100 households can manage several times that number when the routine monitoring is automated, while still giving each client the human contact that a plan for a family, business, and future actually requires. The same shift is visible in how AI is changing financial advisory services, where models draft the analysis and a person delivers the judgment.
The data and security plumbing
The least visible layer is often the most important: identity, permissions, and security. Before a platform can aggregate accounts, the client has to authenticate and grant access, and the platform has to store credentials and balances safely. US firms operate under data protection expectations from regulators and under their own fiduciary duty, so the security layer includes encryption, access controls, and audit logs that record who saw what and when.
This plumbing is also where newer tools are arriving. Some platforms now use machine learning to flag unusual account activity or to draft client communications, and the broader move toward agentic AI tools in finance points toward systems that can carry out multi-step tasks rather than just answer questions. The opportunity is efficiency. The risk is that a system acting on its own can act wrongly at scale, which is why human review stays in the design.
What can go wrong in the workflow
Every layer carries a failure mode. A bad data feed from a custodian can show a client the wrong balance. A flawed assumption in the planning engine can understate how much someone needs to retire. A bug in the rebalancing logic can trade thousands of accounts incorrectly before anyone notices. Because the layers are connected, an error in one can propagate to the next, which is why reconciliation checks, where the system compares its records against the custodian’s, run constantly in the background.
For a firm choosing a platform, the practical test is not how slick the client dashboard looks. It is whether the layers reconcile cleanly, whether the security holds up to audit, and whether a human can override the machine when a client’s situation does not fit the model. Those are the questions that separate a reliable system from a fast one.
How firms choose and connect the pieces
Few firms build all of this in-house. Most assemble a stack from specialist vendors: one tool for planning, another for portfolio accounting, a custodian for settlement, and a client portal on top. Grand View Research lists SS&C Technologies, Fiserv, SEI Investments, and Temenos among the platforms competing to supply these layers. The hard part is the seams. When the planning tool and the accounting system do not share data cleanly, staff end up rekeying figures, which reintroduces exactly the manual errors the software was meant to remove. That is why integration, rather than any single feature, is increasingly the deciding factor in which platform a US firm adopts.
Wealth management technology works best when it is invisible, doing the aggregation, modeling, and rebalancing so smoothly that the client only notices the result. The US firms pulling ahead are the ones treating the technology as a relay to be engineered carefully, not a black box to be trusted blindly.

WASHINGTON, July 18 -- In response to a federal agency request for information, the following public comment letter was submitted electronically to the regulations.gov site.
BAY MILLS INDIAN COMMUNITY WEBSITE: BAYMILLS.ORG
Gnoozhekaaning - Bay Mills Indian Community ("Bay Mills" or the "Tribe") submits this response to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's (the "CFTC") Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (the "ANPR") to express deep concerns regarding the rapid growth of so-called prediction markets, and the practice of operating sports betting or sports wagering businesses on registered exchanges.
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The CFTC issued its ANPR on March 16, 2026 to solicit comments from the public regarding "contract derivatives traded on markets commonly referred to as 'prediction markets.'" These activities are broadly regulated under the framework Congress established in the Commodity Exchange Act, 7 U.S.C. Sub Sec. 1 et seq. (the "CEA").
Bay Mills is concerned with the infringement on its sovereign regulatory powers,
and its ability to generate government revenues, due to the proliferation of these
prediction markets. The Tribe is also concerned about the CFTC's failure to fulfill the
United States' trust obligations to protect tribal regulatory authority over gaming on
tribal lands, and to protect the ability of tribes to generate government revenues
through gaming, as expressed in the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, 25 U.S.C. Sub Sec. 2701
et seq; Pub. L. 100-497 (1988) ("IGRA").
Any regulation or guidance issued by the CFTC regarding prediction markets
must:
1. Affirm that sports wagering has been regulated as "gaming" under other
federal law for decades, including under the IGRA;
2. Preserve the distinct regulatory regime for gaming on Indian lands, including
sports wagering;
3. Prohibit private companies from authorizing, conducting, and regulating
sports wagering and other forms of gaming on Indian lands in violation of
tribal and federal law;
4. Prohibit private companies from engaging in gaming, as defined in IGRA and
associated regulations, on CFTC-regulated exchanges;
5. Prohibit private companies from authorizing, conducting, and regulating
sports wagering on CFTC-regulated exchanges within States in violation of
state laws; and,
6. Prevent private companies from impairing tribal-state gaming compacts
entered into pursuant to IGRA.
Lastly, Bay Mills requests the CFTC to engage in government-to-government
consultations with Indian tribes consistent with E.O. 13175 prior to the issuance or
publication of any proposed rule. As an agency of the Federal Government, the CFTC
shares the United States' trust obligation to protect and advance the interests of Indian
tribes and to engage tribal governments directly on matters that affect their interests.
II. BACKGROUND
Gnoozhekaaning, Bay Mills Indian Community is a federally recognized Indian
tribe located in Michigan's Upper Peninsula near the town of Brimley - approximately
350 miles north of the City of Detroit and approximately 400 miles north of Milwaukee,
Wisconsin (the two nearest major U.S. cities).1 The Bay Mills Indian Reservation is
located entirely within Chippewa County, Michigan, which has a total population of
36,300.
Our Tribe is comprised of approximately 2,400 enrolled tribal citizens, most of
whom reside on or near the Bay Mills Indian Reservation. Those citizens elect a five-
member Executive Council, which adopts tribal laws regulating activities on the Bay
Mills Indian Reservation.
Since the founding of the United States, Bay Mills has entered into three
separate treaties with the United States between 1820 and 1855. Those treaties ceded
millions of acres of lands to the United States, facilitated the admission of the State of
Michigan into the Union, and expressly reserved lands and various other rights for our
tribal citizens. Our Tribe did not receive the final payments for land due under those
treaties until 1997, after Congress passed the Michigan Indian Land Claims Settlement
Act (Pub. L. 105-143).
The people of Bay Mills struggled to find jobs and earn an income on our
remaining homelands on the shores of Lake Superior in the 150 years following our
grant of lands to the United States. The Tribe's government was effectively unable to
generate revenue to support its operations during that time due to the unique laws
limiting tribes' ability to impose taxes to support tribal governments.
To address the lack of jobs and economic opportunity, as well as a need for
governmental revenue, Bay Mills opened the first tribal gaming facility in the State of
1 This is a greater distance than between Washington, D.C. and New York City.
2
Michigan (and one of the first in the nation) on July 4, 1984. Bay Mills successfully
engaged both the U.S. Department of Justice and the State of Michigan in litigation for
years to protect the right of all federally recognized tribes in Michigan to operate and
regulate gaming on tribal lands. In 1993, Bay Mills became one of the first tribes in the
United States to enter into a tribal-state gaming compact under the IGRA. Our Tribe
adopted a tribal gaming ordinance that same year, which was approved by the National
Indian Gaming Commission (the "NIGC").
Today, Bay Mills operates a modest class III gaming facility on our remote
reservation. That gaming facility employs 399 people, including 166 tribal citizens, and
generates important revenue to fund tribal government operations. Our Tribe's efforts
to establish the tribal gaming industry in Michigan paved the way for other federally
recognized tribes in Michigan to engage in gaming. Together, the twelve tribes in
Michigan operate 23 different gaming facilities, employ tens of thousands of people,
and generate approximately $1.5 billion in revenues to provide necessary services to
our tribal citizens. Beyond just benefiting tribal members, tribal gaming facilities
provide $30 million each year to local units of government across Michigan.2
In 2021, Bay Mills became the first tribe in the United States to operate a
statewide online gaming enterprise. This enterprise is licensed and regulated by the
State of Michigan pursuant to the Michigan Lawful Internet Gaming Act, Mich. Comp.
Laws Sub Sec. 432.301 et. seq. (2019), and the Michigan Lawful Sports Betting Act, Mich.
Comp. Laws Sub Sec. 432.401 et. seq. (2019). Each of the twelve federally recognized tribes
in Michigan participates in the statewide online gaming industry, which contributed a
total of $624.5 million in tax revenues to the State of Michigan in 2025.3
Bay Mills's online wagering enterprise reversed a decade of declining tribal
government revenues, and spurred growth in community investments and employment
on our remote reservation.
In 2025, we watched as companies launched nationwide internet sports betting
businesses on CFTC-regulated exchanges. The explosion of these unlawful
nationwide sports betting operations poses a threat to our sovereign authority to
regulate gaming on our own lands, and to vital resources for our tribal government.
2 These amounts are based on publicly available data from the Michigan Gaming Control Board for 2025.
See, Michigan Gaming Control Board Tribal Gaming Report for 2025, (available at:
https://www.michigan.gov/mgcb/-/media/Project/Websites/mgcb/Annual-Reports/2025/2025-Tribal-
Gaming-Report-Final.pdf ).
3 This data is available on the Michigan Gaming Control Board website at:
https://www.michigan.gov/mgcb/detroit-casinos/resources/revenues-and-wagering-tax-information.
3
III. QUESTIONS AND REQUEST FOR COMMENT
The CFTC posed forty categories of questions, many of which contain multiple
sub-questions. Bay Mills has elected to respond to those questions that are most
relevant to our interests as a gaming regulator and a gaming operator. The absence of
a response to any particular question should not be understood as a waiver of any
rights by the Tribe, and the CFTC should not construe the absence of a response to any
particular question as assent to a rulemaking that impairs the Tribe's rights or scope
of our governing authority.
A. Questions on Core Principles and Commission Regulations
The ANPR contains five categories of questions regarding the DCM Core
Principles set forth at 7. U.S.C. Sec. 7(d), and each of those categories include multiple
sub-questions. Bay Mills' comments in this section will correspond to the numbered
categories of questions.
1. Factors the CFTC should consider in determining whether to provide
guidance or amend its regulations regarding how DCM Core Principles
in CEA section 5(d) apply to prediction markets.
As an initial matter, the CFTC must consider the nature and scope of its
statutory authority to regulate activities on exchanges. This includes examining
whether and how its statutory authority conflicts with, or is limited by, other federal
statutes. The ANPR includes questions about potential conflicts with State laws, but
does not attempt to examine potential conflict with other federal laws relating to
Indian tribes and tribal gaming.
There is an entire title of the United States Code devoted to matters involving
Indian tribes, Indian lands, and Indian people; and, there is a well-established body of
corresponding case law interpreting these laws (including conflicts with other federal
statutes).4 That body of law includes the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, and other
statutory provisions that protect tribal governing authority over tribal lands. See, e.g.,
25 U.S.C. Sec. 3651(2)(finding that "Indian tribes are sovereign entities and are
responsible for exercising governmental authority over Indian lands").
As an agency of the Federal Government, the CFTC must ensure that it is
fulfilling its share of the United States' trust and treaty obligations to all federally
recognized Indian tribes and advancing (or avoiding the impairment) of Congress'
policies on matters of Indian affairs.
4 Title 25 of the United States Code.
4
Congress's power to regulate the matters of interstate and international
commerce described in the CEA at 7 U.S.C. Sec. 5 originates in the Commerce Clause of
the Constitution. The Commerce Clause is also the source of Congress's authority to
act in matters of affecting Indian tribes: "The Congress shall have the power[t]o
regulate commerce with foreign nations, and among the several states, and with the
Indian tribes[.]" U.S. Const. Art. I Sec. 8, cl. 3 (emphasis added); see, also Haaland v.
Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255, 273 (2023)("virtually all authority over Indian commerce and
Indian tribes lies with the Federal Government.")(internal quotation and citation
omitted). Congress has broad authority to shape the United States' relationship with
Indian tribes. See, United States v. Jicarilla Apache Nation, 564 U.S. 162, 175
(2011)("the Government has a real and direct interest in the guardianship it exercises
over the Indian tribes; the interest is one which is vested in it as a sovereign.")(internal
quotations omitted).
While the CFTC has both the charge and the authority to advance interstate and
international commerce, it is not free to do so at the expense of Indian tribes and
Congress's declared Indian policies. As explained later in our comments, Congress
has expressly created a federal regulatory framework for gaming on Indian lands. See,
25 U.S.C. Sub Sec. 2701 et. seq. In adopting IGRA, Congress made its intent clear:
The purpose of this chapter is-
(1) to provide a statutory basis for the operation of gaming
by Indian tribes as a means of promoting tribal
economic development, self-sufficiency, and strong
tribal governments;
***
(3) to declare that the establishment of independent Federal
regulatory authority for gaming on Indian lands, the
establishment of Federal standards for gaming on Indian
lands, and the establishment of a National Indian
Gaming Commission are necessary to meet
congressional concerns regarding gaming and to protect
such gaming as a means of generating tribal
revenue.
25 U.S.C. Sec. 2702 (emphasis added).
Congress has charged the Federal Government with the responsibility to protect
the ability of Indian tribes to generate gaming revenues to strengthen tribal
governments and promote economic development. The CFTC is not exempt from this
charge, and cannot ignore it either when considering congressional intent under the
5
CEA, or the adoption of regulations. With respect to "gaming," the CFTC cannot
interpret broad statements in the CEA to effectively repeal IGRA, which was enacted
explicitly to benefit Indian tribes and Indian people. See, Morton v. Mancari, 417 U.S.
535, 550-51 (1974)(holding that courts cannot infer congressional intent to repeal
statutes that abandon its policy of tribal self-government without a clear statement);
and, Swinomish Indian Tribal Community v. BNSF Ry., 951 F.3d 1142, 1156-60 (9th Cir.
2020)(explaining that, in the absence of a clear statement repealing an earlier specific
statute protecting tribal sovereign authority, courts must resolve ambiguities in favor
of tribes).
More specifically, under the direction of Congress as expressed in IGRA, the
CFTC cannot authorize private companies to operate and regulate sports betting
businesses on Indian lands, or authorize those companies to engage in actions that
violate tribal-state agreements approved by the Secretary of the Interior. We discuss
this matter in more detail later in our comments.
2. Factors relevant to prediction markets under Core Principles listed in
the ANPR.5
As an initial matter, the ANPR does not request any feedback regarding the
applicability of Core Principle 16 to the operation and regulation of prediction markets.
Core Principle 16 requires a board of trade to establish and enforce rules to minimize
conflicts of interest in the decision-making process of the market. 7 U.S.C. Sec. 7(d)(16).
Sports wagering carries with it an inherent risk of manipulation, which also
implicates Core Principle 3. This isn't our view alone; it is a view that the CFTC has
previously expressed:
The Commission further notes that most contracts falling
within the proposed definition of "gaming" would have no
underlying cash market with bona fide economic
transactions to provide directly correlated price forming
information. Rather, price forming information is either
nonexistent, or driven by informational sources that are
unregulated, have opaque underlying processes and
procedures, and may not follow scientifically reliable
methodologies. This differs from the informational sources
used for pricing the vast majority of commodities
underlying Commission-regulated derivatives contracts
(e.g., government issued crop forecasts, weather forecasts,
federal government economic data, market-derived supply
5 This category included eight separate sub-questions in the ANPR. In this section, Bay Mills provides
comments on relevant questions contained in this category.
6
and demand metrics for commodities, market-based
interest rate curves). The lack of price forming information
for contracts involving "gaming," or the availability of only
opaque and unregulated sources of price forming
information, may increase the risk of manipulative
activity relating to the trading and pricing of such
contracts, while decreasing the ability of the offering
exchange, or the Commission, to detect such activity.
89 Fed. Reg. 48968, 48982 (June 10, 2024)(emphasis added).
Experienced gaming regulators like Bay Mills (and the State of Michigan)
understand this, and have crafted gaming regulations specifically intended to protect
the integrity of game play and prevent fraud and money laundering. For example, the
Tribe's online sports betting operations are required to partner with independent
monitors to prevent and identify suspicious and manipulative behavior. See, Mich.
Admin. Code r. 432.743.
Prediction market companies run afoul of the CFTC's Core Principles in other
important ways. Some of these companies also own or operate entities that serve as
"market makers" to ensure that there is someone on the other side of the wager in less
popular propositions. In other words, many of these companies finance the wager on
the opposite side of the transaction from people who believe they are wagering against
other customers in the market. This is no different than classic casino gaming, where
patrons bet against the "house."6
In the context of most casino gaming, patrons expect to wager against the
house. They also understand that sportsbooks set odds to maximize the operator's
profits and minimize the operator's losses. These facts highlight the entertainment
and recreational nature of the gaming industry.
With CFTC-regulated entities, users have an expectation that they are trading
with other users - not wagering against the "house" - to hedge risks and discover
prices. CFTC-regulated companies are expected to serve as neutral marketplace
operators, and there is no expectation that they will profit from bettors' losses.
Allowing prediction market companies to have a vested interest in the opposite side of
wagers runs afoul of Core Principles 3, 4 and 16, because the board of trade has a
stake in the outcome of trades, rather than serving as a neutral operator of the market.
This increases the risk of manipulation and price distortion (Core Principles 3 and 4),
and creates a conflict of interest in the decision-making process of the market (Core
6 It is worth noting here that betting against a "house" is not a required element of "gaming." See, e.g., 25
C.F.R. Sec. 501.4(c)(stating that parimutuel wagering is a form of class III gaming).
7
Principle 16). These risks increase for wagers offered to users where there is a limited
number of users available to make the opposite bet, such as for parlays and sporting
events that garner less interest.7
Without a clear separation between the operators of so-called prediction
markets, and the people making trades in those markets, it is difficult for operators to
fulfill their obligations under the Core Principles.
3. Comments pertaining to Institutional traders participating in prediction
markets.
The ANPR includes questions about participation by institutional traders on
prediction markets.
With respect to a gaming activity like sports betting, institutional traders
present several risks. First, their larger positions can materially influence prices,
particularly in low liquidity markets, like parlay bets on very specific propositions.
This influence distorts price discovery. Second, institutional traders benefit from
superior data, analytics, and relationships that create information irregularities and
disadvantage retail bettors. As discussed below, many of the retail bettors in sports
betting markets are teenagers. This asymmetry creates an environment where
institutional traders simply prey upon those teenagers.
These risks amplify concerns around manipulation, conflicts of interest, and the
need for enhanced surveillance and enforceable position limits. The average sports
bettor on a CFTC-regulated exchange does not understand that they are competing
against institutional traders with enormous advantages.
4. Tribal recommendations and requests for the CFTC regarding potential
rulemaking.
Based upon the foregoing, the Tribe makes the following recommendations and
requests of the CFTC:
i. The CFTC must engage in formal, government-to-government
consultations with federally recognized Indian tribes prior to issuing
any proposed rule related to prediction markets. There should be
multiple consultation sessions, with in-person and virtual options to
ensure broad participation. This would facilitate a clearer
7 A number of prediction market companies, including Kalshi, offer users the opportunity to make parlay
bets. Kalshi labels these bets "combos." It defies logic that there are enough betters on these platforms
to take the exact opposite position on these parlay bets. Financing the opposing bet does nothing to
hedge risk or discover prices; instead, it simply mirrors the "house" in a traditional casino.
8
understanding of what factors the CFTC should consider in deciding
whether to provide guidance or amend its regulations.
ii. CFTC legal counsel should engage attorneys from the office of the
Solicitor of the Department of the Interior and the National Indian
Gaming Commission General Counsel to gain an understanding of the
full scope of the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act and its applicability to
sports wagering occurring on Indian lands.
iii. The CFTC must not amend its regulations to authorize sports
wagering on CFTC-regulated exchanges. To the extent the CFTC
believes further guidance or regulations are necessary, it must clarify
that sports wagering is prohibited on regulated exchanges.
iv. The CFTC must prohibit companies from financing bettors or
otherwise serving as the "house" on prediction markets to maintain
the integrity of these markets and comply with Core Principles.
v. The CFTC must prohibit parlay-style sports wagering.
B. Questions Regarding "Public Interest" and "Activities Listed in CEA Section
5c(c)(5)(C)."
The ANPR includes a series of questions relating to the "Public Interest" and
"Activities Listed in CEA Section 5c(c)(5)(C)," which are codified at 7 U.S.C. Sec. 7a-2.
See, 91 Fed. Reg. 12516, 12520-22. Rather than address each question, the Tribe
offers its comment as a more comprehensive discussion on existing federal law
regulating "gaming," and the absence of authority for the CFTC to authorize and
regulate sports wagering and other forms of gaming in light of that law.8
Congress has already established a comprehensive and preemptive regulatory
regime for "gaming" on Indian lands, which includes sports wagering. Indian tribes,
federal agencies, states, and the public have understood "gaming" to encompass
sports wagering for nearly 40 years, and nothing in the CEA has changed that
8 Despite the use of terms like "trade," "swap," "prediction market," or "event contract," many registered
entities understand they are engaging in the operation of sports betting or sports wagering businesses
on their CFTC-registered exchanges. In fact, CFTC lawyers Dave Aron and Matt Jones published an
article in the UNLV Law Journal in 2021 asserting that the CFTC has jurisdiction over some "traditional
sports bets," and that it "can permit sports betting." See, generally, Dave Aron & Matt Jones, States'
Big Gamble on Sports Betting, 12 UNLV L.J. 53, 54, 86 (2021). The article conflates the terms, and uses
the terms "wager," "bet," or "betting" more than 150 times to describe the relevant activity.
9
understanding.9 The CFTC does not have the authority to alter that understanding, or
to diminish the sovereign powers of Indian tribes to authorize, operate, and regulate
gaming on their own lands.
1. Sports wagering has always been regulated as gambling or gaming,
despite sharing similar traits with insurance contracts and financial
derivatives.
Under longstanding common law, gambling was understood to contain three
essential elements: 1) the distribution of a prize; 2) according to chance; 3) in exchange
for consideration. See, e.g., FCC v. American Broadcasting Corp., 347 U.S. 284, 290
(1954). But, these elements are found in a broad range of activities beyond those the
general public considers to be "gambling." For example, many state courts have
wrestled with questions regarding whether pinball machines constituted illegal
gambling devices. See, e.g., Oatman v. Davidson, 310 Mich. 57, 59, 16 N.W.2d 665, 666
(Mich. 1944)(noting that the use of pinball machines involved elements of prize,
chance, and consideration); and, Farina v. Kelly, 147 Conn. 444, 450, 162 A.2d 517, 520
(Conn. 1960)("A coin operated pinball machine which is designed to provide free plays
upon the scoring of certain numbers or combinations of numbers is a gaming device").
Other activities, like entering into contracts to insure property or trading on the
future price of a commodity, also involve elements of consideration, chance, and prize.
The law has long distinguished between gambling and insurance contracts, while early
state laws regulating gambling applied to speculative trading in commodity futures.
See, Bd. of Trade of City of Chicago v. Christie Grain & Stock Co., 198 U.S. 236, 247-48,
(1905); and, Brian M. McCall, Gambling on Our Financial Future: How the Federal
Government Fiddles While State Common Law Is A Safer Bet to Prevent Another
Financial Collapse, 46 Ariz. St. L.J. 1347, 1371-76 (2014).
Over the last century, the federal government and states have developed
regulatory regimes that distinguish between "gambling" (or "gaming"), insurance
contracts, and financial derivatives. The laws governing these different activities have
evolved separately, despite sharing similar characteristics involving the payment of
consideration for the chance to receive a prize (i.e. something of value). See, Timothy
E. Lynch, Coming Up Short: The United States' Second-Best Strategies for Corralling
Purely Speculative Derivatives, 36 Cardozo L. Rev. 545, 580-82 (2014). Insurance
contracts are largely regulated pursuant to state law, whereas financial derivatives
have come to be regulated under laws like the CEA and the Securities Exchange Act.
9 In fact, federal statute prohibited expanded sports wagering throughout the United States at the time
the CEA was amended in 2010 to include the definition of "swap." See, Professional and Amateur Sports
Protection Act, Pub. L. 102-559, 28 U.S.C. Sub Sec. 3701-3704 ("PASPA") (held unconstitutional in
unconstitutional in Murphy v. Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n., 584 U.S. 453 (2018)).
10
Gaming activities have historically been regulated by the states as well. To the
extent that Congress and the Federal Government have chosen to regulate gaming, it
has often based enforcement of federal law on the application of state gaming laws.
See, e.g., 18 U.S.C. Sec. 1084(b)(stating that criminal prohibitions do not apply to
wagering transmissions from one state to another where such wagers are legal); and,
31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(10)(prohibiting wagers over the internet based upon prohibitions in
state law where the bet is initiated and received)("UIGEA"). Even IGRA relies on state
gaming laws for its regulatory regime. IGRA states that tribes may only authorize,
operate, and regulate gaming on their lands if "such Indian gaming is located within a
State that permits such gaming." 25 U.S.C. Sec. 2710(b)(1)(A).
The Federal Government has long understood that wagering on sports events -
including the outcome, performance of athletes, point spreads, etc. - constituted
gaming, and was not regulated as a financial derivative. See, e.g., 28 U.S.C. Sec. 3702
(prohibiting wagers on "one or more competitive games in which amateur or
professional athletes participate, or are intended to participate, or on one or more
performances of such athletes in such games.").10 The Federal Government also has a
long history of prosecuting people involved in illegal sports wagering under federal
gambling statutes. See, e.g., United States v. Kaczowski, 114 F. Supp.2d 143 (W.D.N.Y.
2000); and, United States v. Giovanelli, 747 F.Supp. 897 (S.D.N.Y. 1989).
UIGEA is a particularly notable statute, because many companies operating
sports betting businesses on CFTC-regulated exchanges point to UIGEA as a tacit
authorization to offer sports betting. In defining the term "bet or wager" in UIGEA,
Congress created 9 different exemptions from the term. See, 31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(1)(E).
UIGEA does, in fact, expressly exempt transactions that are "excluded or exempt from
regulation under the Commodity Exchange Act[.]" 31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(1)(E)(iv)(I).
Nevertheless, three other provisions in the same section of UIGEA make it clear that
Congress took steps to ensure that UIGEA could not be used to authorize sports
wagering in jurisdictions that prohibit it.
For example, 31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(1)(E) also exempts certain fantasy sports contests
from its scope. But that exemption is conditioned on the winning outcome of a fantasy
sports contest not being based:
(aa) on the score, point-spread, or any performance or
performances of any single real-world team or any
combination of such teams; or
10 In its decision in Murphy, the Supreme Court acknowledged the authority of states to regulate sports
wagering. See, Id. at 486 ("Congress can regulate sports gambling directly, but if it elects not to do so,
each State is free to act on its own.").
11
(bb) solely on any single performance of an individual
athlete in any single real-world sporting or other event.
31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(1)(E)(ix)(III).
Section 5362 also states that intrastate wagers would not constitute unlawful
internet gaming, provided that they comply with state law and do not violate any
provision of PASPA or IGRA. See, 31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(10)(B) (emphasis added). UIGEA
also exempts the activities of financial institutions, but expressly states that the term
"financial institutiondoes not include a casino, sports book, or other business at or
through which bets or wagers may be placed or received." 31 U.S.C. Sec. 5362(11)(C). It
strains credulity to read UIGEA as a tacit authorization for sports wagering on a CFTC-

did not authorize sports wagering where tribes and states prohibit it.
Nothing in the CEA references any other federal statute governing gambling or
modifies the longstanding view of the Federal Government that sports wagering is
governed under laws and regulations applicable to gaming.
The CFTC has not been delegated any authority to alter the longstanding
regulatory regime governing gaming or sports wagering in the United States. It simply
may not assert authority to promulgate regulations that attempt to regulate sports
wagering as a financial derivative.
2. Indian Tribes and Federal Agencies have been regulating sports
wagering as "gaming" under statute for nearly 40 years.
Congress amended the CEA in 2010 to include the "Special Rule" for event
contracts. See, Pub. L. 111-203, 7 U.S.C. Sec. 7a-2(c)(5)(C). By that time, it had long
understood that "gaming" had a clear meaning under federal law (and not just state
laws).
In the early 1980's the Federal Government provided financial support for the
development of tribal gaming facilities, and exercised some regulatory authority to
review ordinances that tribal governments had adopted to regulate gaming on their
lands. See, California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians, 480 U.S. 202, 218
(1987)(noting agency financial support for the development of tribal gaming facilities,
and the Secretary of the Interior's approval of tribal gaming ordinances). In 1987, the
United States Supreme Court affirmed that tribal governments had the authority to
authorize, operate, and regulate "gaming" activities on their lands. See, Id. The Court
based its reasoning, in part, on the "important federal interests" in the potential for
gaming to promote tribal self-sufficiency." See, Id. at 217.
12
The following year, in 1988, Congress adopted IGRA. The entire focus of IGRA
was to establish a federal regulatory framework for the tribal gaming industry. Federal
courts have consistently held that IGRA is both comprehensive and preemptive, when
it comes to the regulation of "gaming" on Indian lands. See, Gaming Corp. of America
v. Dorsey & Whitney, 88 F.3d 536, 548 (8th Cir. 1996)(holding that Congress intended for
IGRA to have extraordinary preemptive force).11
Among other things, IGRA divides "gaming" into three separate classes, and
provides definitions for them. "Class III" gaming includes all forms of gaming that
aren't: tribal cultural games, bingo, or certain card games. 25 U.S.C. Sec. 2703(8). The
language of IGRA is explicit that class III gaming "is lawful on Indian lands only if such
activities" are authorized by a tribe and regulated in accordance with IGRA. 25 U.S.C.
Sec. 2710(d)(1)(emphasis added). Tribes have the primary authority to authorize gaming
on their own lands and regulate that gaming in accordance with their own laws.
IGRA also established a federal regulatory agency - the National Indian Gaming
Commission (the "NIGC") - devoted to the regulation of "gaming" on Indian lands. See,
25 U.S.C. Sub Sec. 2704 to 2718 (emphasis added). The NIGC's power includes the authority
to review and approve tribal gaming ordinances. See, 25 U.S.C. Sec. 2710.
The NIGC has been exercising its statutory powers for nearly four decades in a
manner that confirms sports wagering is a form of "gaming," under IGRA. For
example, the NIGC has promulgated regulations defining the scope of the term
"gaming." See, 25 C.F.R. Sub Sec. 501. Those regulations state:

C. Questions Regarding "Inside Information."
The ANPR poses a number of questions regarding "inside information,"
including a question about whether there is "public interest utility" if people with "an
asymmetric information advantage" are able to place bets on prediction markets. The
Tribe understands that the CFTC is seeking information on this issue, and that some
academics believe that there is utility to allowing insiders to make trades (or bets)
based on their access to information that others in the market don't have. That may be
true in a laboratory setting, but it creates enormous risks in a federally regulated
public exchange.
In December 2025, the CEO for the prediction market operator Coinbase, made
a public statement stating that "insider trading" on prediction markets was desirable.
Will Gottsegen, The Polymarket Bets on Maduro Are a Warning, The Atlantic (Jan. 6,
2026).24 Since those remarks, there have been a number of instances where suspicious
activity led to enormous payouts on a number of prediction markets. See, Benjamin
Weiser and Jonah E. Bromwich, Soldier Used Classified Information to Bet on
Maduro's Ouster, U.S. Says, New York Times (April 23, 2026). Insider trading not only
creates an insurmountable financial advantage for those using their "asymmetric
information advantage" in a public market, but it also creates the risk that people will
manipulate events to gain a profit. Rather than disclosing the "price" of an outcome, it
manipulates the price altogether.

The $53B Stablecoin Endgame appeared first on Memeburn.
Why Would Stripe Buy PayPal? The $53B Stablecoin Endgame ACI Information Group
Stripe and Advent International have jointly offered $60.50 per share to acquire PayPal Holdings, valuing the company at more than $53 billion in what would be the largest fintech acquisition ever attempted. The bid, first reported by Reuters and the Financial Times on July 15, carries approximately $50 billion in committed bank financing and proposes equal ownership between Stripe and Advent, with no plan to break up PayPal.
The offer represents a 28% premium over PayPal’s July 14 closing price of $47.37. PayPal shares surged roughly 17% on the news, closing at $55.52, still about 9% below the bid price. Stripe, Advent, and Block are contributing approximately $17 billion in equity, CNBC reported. PayPal has not publicly responded to the offer.
The question that has dominated analyst notes and prediction markets since the news broke is straightforward. Stripe was valued at $159 billion in a February 2026 tender offer. It processed $1.9 trillion in total payment volume last year, surpassing PayPal’s $1.79 trillion for the first time. Why would a company that already outgrew its rival spend $53 billion to acquire it?
What Stripe and Advent Actually Offered
Apr 2026 Stripe and Advent approach PayPal. Board does not respond
Jun 30, 2026 Stripe leads launch of Open USD stablecoin consortium with 140+ partners
Early Jul 2026 Formal $60.50 offer submitted
Jul 15, 2026 Reuters and FT report the bid. PYPL closes up 17.2% at $55.52
Jul 20, 2026 PayPal board expected to meet (reported by CNBC)
Jul 28, 2026 PayPal Q2 2026 earnings report
~End Jul 2026 Stripe and Advent target deadline to advance talks
Why Would Stripe Buy PayPal?
Stripe owns the merchant side of digital payments. Over one million businesses use its infrastructure to accept payments, but the company has never built a large consumer-facing product. PayPal’s 439 million active accounts and Venmo’s peer-to-peer network represent the consumer side that Stripe’s merchant stack cannot replicate organically.
The acquisition logic extends beyond user count. Sanjay Sakhrani, analyst at Keefe Bruyette & Woods, wrote in a July 15 research note that PayPal’s consumer data would be an advantage “in the world of agentic commerce,” referring to AI systems that transact autonomously on behalf of users. Bryan Bergin at TD Cowen added that PayPal would accelerate Stripe’s expansion of Link, its one-click checkout and consumer wallet, which Stripe has been positioning for agentic payments.
Combined payment volume would reach approximately $3.7 trillion per year, roughly 3% of global GDP, making the merged entity the largest U.S. merchant acquirer by volume. Market analyst Simon Taylor framed it this way: last year was the first time Stripe’s payment volume surpassed PayPal’s, and nine months later, Stripe bid for the whole company.
The Stablecoin Angle That Finance Coverage Is Missing
Stripe has spent two years assembling a stablecoin infrastructure stack. It acquired Bridge, a stablecoin orchestration platform, for $1.1 billion in a deal that closed in February 2025. Bridge received conditional OCC approval to issue and custody stablecoins. Stripe then launched Tempo, a payments-focused blockchain built with Paradigm.
On June 30, Stripe led the launch of Open USD, a GENIUS Act-compliant stablecoin backed by a consortium of more than 140 companies including Mastercard, Coinbase, Visa, and BlackRock. Stripe committed to making Open USD its default stablecoin. The design shares reserve earnings with partners, directly challenging Circle’s USDC and Tether’s USDT economics. Circle’s stock dropped 17% on the announcement.
PayPal brings its own crypto stack. PYUSD, a dollar-denominated stablecoin issued by Paxos Trust, had a market capitalization of approximately $2.85 billion as of mid-July 2026, according to multiple sources, though estimates vary. CoinDesk cited a CoinGecko figure of $185 million, while TechTimes and The Defiant placed the figure closer to $2.8-2.85 billion, a discrepancy likely reflecting different tracking methodologies across on-chain aggregators. PYUSD operates across nine blockchain networks and reached 70 markets by March 2026.
If the deal closes, one owner would control Bridge (stablecoin orchestration), Tempo (settlement blockchain), PYUSD (consumer-facing stablecoin), and a leadership role in Open USD. That combination covers issuance, settlement, and consumer checkout in a single entity. No existing payments company holds that full stack. For Circle, which already lost 17% on the Open USD announcement, the addition of PYUSD’s distribution network to Stripe’s infrastructure would represent a second competitive pressure point.
Not Everyone Buys the Logic
Jefferies analyst Trevor Williams said the combined entity would primarily target consumer payments, calling the competitive impact on rivals like Adyen roughly “neutral.” BTIG, by contrast, called the offer a “lifeline worth taking,” arguing that PayPal is in “no-man’s land” amid a leadership change and would benefit from going private.
The valuation fight is where sharper disagreement sits. Michael Burry called the $60.50 bid “simply too low” in a Substack post on July 15. Burry, who purchased PayPal shares at $49 and again at $40 over the prior three months, estimated intrinsic value between $75 and $115 per share, with a best estimate near $100. Thomas Hayes of Great Hill Capital argued that even an offer above $80 would undervalue PayPal.
PayPal’s stock behavior supports the skeptics. PYPL closed at $55.52, roughly 9% below the $60.50 offer. In a standard take-private with high closing probability, the discount typically runs 2-5%. A 9% spread suggests the market believes the deal may not close at the current price. PayPal’s decline from a 2021 peak market cap of roughly $360 billion to as low as $36 billion in 2026 reinforces the argument that $60.50 is an opening bid.
Will the Stripe PayPal Acquisition Actually Close?
Polymarket traders assign an 82% probability that PayPal is acquired before the end of 2027, and approximately 74% that Stripe specifically closes a deal in 2026. In March, when antitrust concerns dominated, odds sat around 18%. The jump to 82% reflects the progression from speculation to a formal, fully financed bid.
Several variables remain unresolved. The PayPal board is expected to meet as early as July 20. PayPal’s Q2 earnings on July 28 could shift the board’s leverage, with a strong quarter strengthening the case for independence and a weak one reducing it.
Antitrust scrutiny is another open variable. Combined processing volume of $3.7 trillion would draw attention from the FTC and European regulators. Analysts have noted that divestitures of Braintree or Venmo could be required as a condition of approval. Blair estimated that Stripe and Advent could go as high as $70 per share if pressed, though it assigned low probability to that outcome.
What Comes Next
Three scenarios cover the range of outcomes.
If the deal closes near the current terms, PayPal’s crypto assets fold into Stripe’s infrastructure, creating a unified payments and stablecoin settlement platform with consumer distribution that no competitor currently matches. PYPL would be delisted, and Circle would face a combined entity with $3.7 trillion in annual volume and multiple stablecoin products competing for settlement dominance.
If the board counters with a higher price, the deal still likely closes but at a number closer to Burry’s $75-$100 range, particularly if Q2 earnings on July 28 give Lores credible evidence of a standalone turnaround. The stablecoin integration timeline would stretch but the strategic logic would remain the same.
If the deal collapses, whether through regulatory intervention, financing withdrawal, or board rejection, PayPal returns to its pre-bid trajectory. PYUSD would continue operating independently, and Stripe would rely on Bridge, Tempo, and Open USD without the consumer-facing distribution layer that PayPal’s 439 million accounts provide.
The next data points arrive within two weeks. The board meeting around July 20, the Stripe-Advent target deadline at month’s end, and PayPal’s Q2 earnings on July 28 will determine whether the $60.50 figure holds, rises, or becomes irrelevant.
FAQs
Why would Stripe buy PayPal if Stripe already processes more payments?
Stripe handles more merchant payment volume than PayPal but has no large consumer-facing wallet or user base. PayPal’s 439 million active accounts and Venmo give Stripe access to the consumer side of payments, completing a two-sided network it cannot build as quickly on its own.
Is $60.50 per share a fair price for PayPal?
Opinions are divided. Michael Burry estimated PayPal’s intrinsic value between $75 and $115 per share, with a best estimate near $100. PayPal’s stock closed at $55.52, about 9% below the bid, suggesting the market expects the deal to happen but not necessarily at the current price.
What happens to PYUSD if Stripe buys PayPal?
PYUSD, PayPal’s dollar stablecoin issued by Paxos, would likely be integrated into Stripe’s broader stablecoin infrastructure, which includes Bridge, the Tempo blockchain, and a leading role in the Open USD consortium. The combined entity would control both issuance and consumer distribution of stablecoin assets.
Will regulators block the Stripe PayPal acquisition?
Antitrust review by the FTC and European regulators is expected given the combined $3.7 trillion in annual payment volume. Analysts have flagged potential divestitures of Braintree or Venmo as conditions for approval, but no regulatory filing has been made public yet.

WASHINGTON, July 17 (TNSletter) -- Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts, ranking member of the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, issued the following letter to the Senate leadership:
* * *
Here is the text of the letter:
July 13, 2026
The Honorable John Thune
Majority Leader
United States Senate
Dear Leader Thune and Minority Leader Schumer:
On June 30, 2026, the Office of Government Ethics released President Trump's Public Financial Disclosure Report for 2025.1 That report revealed that in 2025 alone, the President made roughly $1.4 billion from his cryptocurrency ventures - more than double his total income in 2024 and more than any publicly traded U.S. crypto company earned last year.2 Indeed, crypto now accounts for the vast majority of the President's income.3 This new disclosure is particularly troubling as the President urges Congress to pass cryptocurrency deregulation legislation that will almost certainly boost the value of his crypto holdings.
The disclosure also demonstrates the extent to which President Trump's family is profiting off of their crypto businesses. "Trump Family Members," for example, have a 30% ownership stake in "DT Marks Defi LLC," a cryptocurrency venture that includes "Coinbase accounts" worth over $100 million and a "38.25% ownership interest in WLF Holdco LLC."4 "WLF Holdco LLC" owns "the only membership interest in World Liberty Financial, Inc.," the cryptocurrency company founded by President Trump and his sons.5 DT Marks Defi LLC alone generated over $590 million in income in 2025.6 "Trump Family Members" also have an ownership stake, via an LLC intermediary, in "Stablecoin Holdco LLC," the President's "Stablecoin business."7 As a reminder, Americans are currently struggling with the cost of gas, groceries, and housing, with credit card and auto delinquency rates at record highs.8
Concerningly, unknown "Third Parties" also own a significant portion of the President's cryptocurrency business. Specifically, "Third Parties" own a 61.75% stake in both Stablecoin Holdco LLC and WLF Holdco LLC.9 This disclosure comes in the wake of reports from earlier this year showing that "[f]our days before Donald Trump's inauguration" in 2025, affiliates of United Arab Emirates (UAE) National Security Advisor Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan "signed a deal with the Trump family to purchase a 49% stake in" World Liberty Financial, the crypto business held by WLF Holdco LLC. According to the financial disclosure, that deal generated a whopping $263 million windfall for the President.10
The President's 2025 financial disclosure was released as the U.S. Senate debates crypto market structure legislation. Despite the many hours the Senate is devoting to this issue, recent public opinion polling suggests that the American public is far more concerned with the affordability crisis exacerbated by President Trump's disastrous economic agenda. According to a survey by crypto news outlet CoinDesk, "Crypto is at the bottom of U.S. voters' priority heading into elections." Just 1% of respondents ranked crypto as their top concern, compared to 36% of respondents citing the cost of living, 13% citing jobs and the economy, and 11% citing Social Security and Medicare.11 But rather than addressing Americans' real concerns, the Senate appears to be prioritizing legislation that could further boost the Trump family's crypto businesses.
Leader Thune has indicated he aims to hold a floor vote on crypto market structure legislation this month, despite significant flaws in the current draft that have raised concerns about risks to national security, financial stability, consumer protection, and ethics. Those concerns have become even more pressing in light of the President's 2025 financial disclosure, which underscores the severity of his crypto-related conflicts of interest. The crypto legislation heading to the Senate floor must prevent the President, Vice President, senior administration officials, members of Congress, and their families from profiting off the crypto industry. Anything less would be a flagrant giveaway to the President and his family at the expense of the public.
Sincerely,
Elizabeth Warren, Ranking Member, Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

headline: Do You Really ‘Own’ Crypto If the Government Can Just Take It?
detail_text:
Do You Really ‘Own’ Crypto If the Government Can Just Take It?
Matched:
COIN
Source: DeFi Planet
Publication Date: 7/18/2026 5:22:43 AM
During a Fox Business interview on May 29, 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US government, as at May 2026, had cumulatively seized roughly $1 billion in crypto tied to Iranian entities, the largest sanctions-related crypto grab on record.
Do You Really ‘Own’ Crypto If the Government Can Just Take It? ACI Information Group
Iran and the US have had frosty relations for the better part of the last half-century, and like many other foes of the US and its allies, sanctions, economic and otherwise, as well as asset seizures, are very common. Crypto, while definitely qualifying as an asset that can be seized, has a bit of a different ring to it.
Anyone who’s read Bitcoin’s whitepaper can sense that one of Satoshi Nakamoto’s major motivations for creating Bitcoin after the 2008 financial crisis was to build an instrument of value transfer that no single entity had full control over, one nobody could manipulate on a whim. Anonymity, speed, efficiency, cutting out the middlemen, that was the whole pitch.
Now that it has been established that governments can legally track, swoop in, and seize virtually any type of cryptoassets, what then are the real limits of crypto’s pseudonymity?
Governments are getting better at tracking, restricting, and confiscating crypto tied to sanctioned or illegal activity. Is crypto ownership genuinely independent, or does it still answer to the same legal systems as a bank account? And if cryptoassets can be reached by a government at this scale, is there still a credible case for marketing privacy as one of crypto’s advantages over traditional institutions like banks?
What Happened in the $1 Billion Iranian Crypto Seizure
Can governments seize cryptocurrency? Speaking at the Reagan National Economic Forum, the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the crypto seizure operation involved taking control of digital wallets believed to be connected to sanctioned Iranian networks.
“I believe that we have seized about a billion dollars of their crypto,” Bessent said. “Just outright grabbed the wallets. Some of them may be typing in right now and not have realized that their wallet had been grabbed.”
US Seizes $1 Billion in Iranian Crypto, Says Bessent
The seizure is part of a US sanctions campaign against Iran known as Operation Economic Fury, launched in March 2025. The operation targets Iranian financial channels across crypto, banking, and international assets, restricting funding flows linked to the regime.
According to Bessent, the campaign aims to cut off financial support networks that were reportedly moving hundreds of millions of dollars each month.
“I think between five and a half to six weeks of an incredibly successful military campaign and Operation Economic Fury, where we have really cut them off. They are at the end of their tether now financially.”
The Treasury Department insists that these measures are necessary because Iran’s financial system is under severe pressure, with high inflation, reduced payments to military personnel, and internal funding constraints.
How Crypto Seizures Actually Work in Practice
Crypto seizures depend heavily on where and how the assets are stored, because not all crypto is equally accessible to authorities.
There is a big difference between custodial wallets and self-custodied wallets.
Custodial wallets are held by exchanges or regulated platforms that can be ordered by courts or regulators to freeze or transfer funds. For example, if crypto is stored on a centralized exchange like Coinbase or Binance, authorities can work with those platforms to block access or move assets once legal orders are issued.
Self-custodied wallets, on the other hand, are controlled directly by private keys held by individuals, which makes them much harder to access unless the keys are obtained through investigation or legal pressure.
To trace and locate assets, authorities rely on blockchain analytics tools and forensic tracking systems from firms such as Chainalysis and Elliptic.
Chainalysis website interface. Source: Chainalysis
These tools allow investigators to follow transaction flows across wallets, identify patterns, and link addresses to real-world entities when crypto eventually touches regulated exchanges. This is often how funds are tracked, even when users try to move them through multiple wallets or mixing services.
Once identified, crypto assets can be frozen, seized, or recovered, depending on the level of control authorities have. If the assets are on a regulated platform, they can be frozen through compliance systems. If they are linked to criminal or sanctioned activity, authorities may obtain court approval to transfer the assets into government-controlled wallets.
The key point is that digital asset ownership does not automatically mean full immunity from US crypto sanctions enforcement. While blockchain technology allows peer-to-peer control, the system still interacts with regulated exchanges, banks, and legal frameworks.
Does Government Enforcement Strengthen or Weaken Trust in Digital Assets?
The US crypto sanctions enforcement creates a split view. On one side, it can make the industry look more legitimate. On the other hand, it raises questions about how neutral and independent digital assets really are.
Arguments that enforcement increases institutional confidence
When authorities take action against illegal activity, it signals that crypto is not outside the financial system but part of it.
For example, the US Department of Justice’s seizure of Bitcoin linked to the 2016 Bitfinex hack (where authorities recovered billions in stolen BTC years later) showed that law enforcement can track and recover stolen assets even long after the crime.
Similarly, when Binance reached a settlement with U.S. regulators in 2023 over compliance failures, it removed some uncertainty around how large exchanges are expected to operate under financial law. For institutions, this kind of clarity can reduce perceived risk and make regulated participation more comfortable.
Concerns that aggressive crypto seizures could reduce confidence in financial neutrality
Another challenge is the potential for enforcement to reduce trust in the financial impartiality of crypto assets. This can be illustrated with the case of US sanctions imposed on Tornado Cash in 2022. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the enforcement arm of the U.S. Treasury Department, added the protocol to its sanctions list, claiming it had been used to launder more than $7.6 billion in virtual assets since its creation in 2019, including funds tied to the Lazarus Group.
Tornado Cash challenged the designation, and in November 2024, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in its favour. The court found that OFAC had overstepped its authority by sanctioning the mixer, on the grounds that immutable smart contracts are not the property of a foreign national or entity and therefore cannot be blocked under sanctions law.
Rather than appeal, the Treasury Department chose to drop the case. In March 2025, OFAC officially lifted the sanctions on Tornado Cash, removing the protocol and its associated wallet addresses from the sanctions list. Treasury framed the move as discretionary rather than a concession, saying it had “exercised its discretion to remove the economic sanctions” in light of the “novel legal and policy issues” the case raised, while reiterating that it would keep targeting the use of crypto for money laundering and sanctions evasion by state actors like North Korea.
The delisting did not close the broader saga. Criminal charges against Tornado Cash co-founder Roman Storm remain separate from the sanctions case and are proceeding on their own track, while developer Roman Semenov remains under a separate sanctions designation tied to North Korea.
The episode is now a clearer data point than it was in 2022. A US appeals court drew a legal line between sanctioning a person or entity and sanctioning autonomous code, and the Treasury Department accepted that line rather than fight it further. For crypto, that is a meaningful precedent: it shows the legal system can constrain how far enforcement reaches into decentralized infrastructure, even while individual developers and entities connected to that infrastructure remain fair game.
Transparency, Control, and What “Safety” Really Means in Crypto
Although crypto is said to be transparent and secure, this doesn’t necessarily mean that people can control assets or results since visibility is not always linked to control.
Why blockchain transparency makes tracking possible
Blockchain public networks, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, create an unchangeable log of each operation performed. Therefore, anyone can see how the funds move within wallets.
For instance, if there is any suspicious activity, such as theft, authorities can track the flow of money even if someone moves the funds fast or to another wallet, trying to cover the trail.
The difference between visibility and real control over assets
A person using a self-custodied wallet retains full control over their assets, as long as they hold the private keys. However, when funds are involved in operations where centralized platforms are used, things become quite tricky.
Visibility does not always mean control. Someone can watch a transaction happen in real time and still be powerless to stop it.
The tradeoff between regulatory oversight and financial autonomy
With better monitoring, safety is enhanced by preventing fraudulent activities such as money laundering and sanctions violations. However, there are implications for user independence when this happens.
As cryptocurrency becomes more deeply embedded in the existing financial framework, its vulnerability to legal scrutiny increases. The question that users face is whether it’s worth sacrificing their financial autonomy for protection and enforcement.
What This Means for Global Users, Institutions, and the Future of Crypto Regulation
The enforcement activities related to crypto do not remain localized. In fact, enforcement activity in one jurisdiction affects the behaviour of users and companies all around the world.
Effects on international adoption and international transfers
Improved enforcement might give users confidence in using cryptocurrency for day-to-day transactions, particularly for international transfers, where understanding regulations becomes critical. For instance, if leading exchanges ensure they follow the guidelines of both the U.S. and the EU, they become more acceptable to banks and other payment networks. Yet, enhanced regulations could hinder adoption in other jurisdictions by increasing costs when transferring crypto assets abroad.
How institutions may view enforcement as reducing risk
For financial institutions, including banks, asset managers, and payments companies, enforcement is seen as a means of lowering uncertainty by providing clarity as to what actions will not be tolerated within their domain. This is one of the reasons why big organizations have been more willing to invest in cryptocurrencies, because the laws governing crypto are becoming strict enough for the industry to move away from its shady practices and into mainstream finance.
Whether stricter sanctions enforcement could push activity toward alternative systems or privacy tools
At the same time, this could also make individuals look into using systems where their identity is protected more strictly. This was shown by the sanctions against Tornado Cash and their warning that the enforcement of such policies could drive those who have intentions to remain private to utilize more decentralized networks.
The New Reality of Crypto Ownership in a Regulated World
The crypto confiscation case in Iran highlights that the crypto ecosystem can no longer remain an independent world of its own. Through the use of advanced tracking technologies, along with cooperation with crypto exchanges and the crypto network itself, the authorities ensure that digital currencies are as accountable as fiat currencies.
Looking ahead, the most significant change will no longer revolve around the controllability of crypto but rather around its predictability in enforcement. As the process becomes more standardized, the market will likely come up with a way to account for this form of risk management. The result is a crypto market that is less “outside the system” and more deeply integrated into it, with all the tradeoffs that come with that shift.

Does blockchain transparency make it easier for authorities than traditional banking investigations?
Could stricter enforcement slow down crypto innovation?

AI’s IPO boom is creating venture capital’s biggest winners ACI Information Group
Venture capital’s biggest winners are changing the rules of the exit game, and 2026’s IPO boom is allowing them to cash in. US IPOs have reportedly already raised more than $141.2 billion this year. This puts the market within striking distance of the $142.4 billion record set in 2021. The biggest artificial intelligence listings are still expected to come.
For private equity firms investing in these firms, the time is virtually perfect. However, this might not be the case for long. Brookfield-backed data center operator Csquare is looking to raise up to $1.35 billion under its IPO scheduled for July 15, which may push the fundraising this year to a level never seen before. Nuclear startup Standard Nuclear is also aiming for its debut on that day and is trying to raise the amount of $384.3 million.
Widening the gap with the AI elite
There are even greater names ready to enter the scene. Stelios Saffos, partner at Latham & Watkins, told Axios that the recent boom of large offerings has been “as much of a green light as you could possibly get.” According to him, the investors jumped into these deals partially due to their beliefs that such companies as Anthropic and OpenAI will follow suit.
Venture investing generates billions of dollars for investors, their institutions and creates millions of jobs. Many venture-backed companies have scaled, gone public, and become household names, and at the same time have generated high-skilled jobs and trillions of dollars of benefit for the U.S. economy.
It states that jobs at VC-supported companies increased by 960% between 1990 and 2020 compared to 40% in the overall economy and estimates that three-quarters of the largest venture capital-funded companies would not have grown to that extent had they not received venture financing. However, at this point one question becomes practically impossible to evade: how much of the current AI-driven growth is going to benefit companies that are not in the top rankings?
Still, the rally is fraught with dangers. As Axios pointed out, there’s growing interconnectedness to AI investment. The same hype that has reignited the IPO market can just as quickly reverse if investor mood soured.
A case in point: Tim Draper is a third-generation Silicon Valley venture capitalist and founder of Draper Fisher Jurvetson, Draper University and Draper Associates. A Stanford University electrical-engineering graduate with an MBA from Harvard Business School, he founded Draper Associates in 1985. He’s since been a backer of more than 60 “unicorns” at the seed stage, including Tesla, SpaceX, Twitch, Coinbase Global, Robinhood and Baidu. He weighs in on the AI bubble and four huge opportunities he missed.
In a recent interview, Draper shares how he identifies ideas that seem impossible, where he sees the next wave of AI opportunity, whether AI stocks are in a bubble and why he refuses to make a bear case — for anything. He compared AI’s current trajectory to the early internet era. His notable remark: “I invest in heroes.”
Is there a new order in the venture capital sector?
Other areas still continue to face difficulty. The Financial Times states London has achieved its lowest amount of money raised from IPOs in the last 30 years, which means investment banks and advisers have to count more on private markets, while asking policymakers to make changes. The situation has created the greatest difference between regions: record fundraising in New York due to AI while listing markets are still stuck elsewhere.
The next significant trial will occur when OpenAI and Anthropic eventually enter the public market. Their IPOs will show if the venture capital companies that supported them from the beginning can turn years of unrealistic profits into actual gains and solidify a new order in the venture capital sector.

Applicable Legislative Provisions

While registered as a restricted dealer, the Filer will apply to become registered as an investment dealer and seek membership with CIRO.
This Decision has been tailored for the specific facts and circumstances of the Filer, and the securities regulatory authority or regulator in the Jurisdictions will not consider this Decision as constituting a precedent for other filers.

Operation of the Platform
32. A Crypto Contract is a bilateral contract between a Client and the Filer. Accordingly, the Filer is a counterparty to all trades entered by Clients on the Platform. For each Client transaction, the Filer is also a counterparty to one or more corresponding Crypto Asset buy or sell transactions with a Liquidity Provider.
33. Clients enter into Crypto Contracts with the Filer and resulting transactions are conducted through the Website or App. Clients are able to submit orders, either in units of the applicable Crypto Asset or in fiat currency, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Clients are able to deposit and withdraw certain Crypto Assets and Canadian dollars, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week (or where applicable, for fiat currency, during banking hours).
34. The Filer establishes, maintains, and applies policies and procedures that identify and address conflicts of interest arising from the operation of the Platform and its related services in the best interest of its Clients, including conflicts between the interests of its owners, its commercial interests, and the responsibilities and sound functioning of the Platform and related services.
35. The Filer currently relies on multiple Liquidity Providers to act as a seller of Crypto Assets that may be purchased by the Filer for its Clients. The Liquidity Providers may also buy any Crypto Assets from the Filer that Clients wish to sell.
36. The Filer evaluates the prices obtained from its Liquidity Providers on an ongoing basis against global benchmarks to provide fair and reasonable pricing to its Clients.
37. The Filer has taken reasonable steps to verify that each Liquidity Provider is appropriately registered or licensed to trade in the Crypto Assets in its home jurisdiction, or that its activities do not require registration or licensing in its home jurisdiction, and that the Liquidity Provider is not in default of securities legislation in the Jurisdictions. The Filer also assesses liquidity and concentration risks posed by the Liquidity Provider.
38. The Filer has verified that each Liquidity Provider has effective policies and procedures to address concerns relating to fair price, fraud, and market manipulation.
39. After a Client requests a quote for the purchase or sale of a Crypto Asset from the Filer, the Filer obtains a price for the Crypto Asset from a Liquidity Provider, after which the Filer incorporates a spread to compensate the Filer, and presents this total cost to the Client.
40. If the Client is agreeable, the Client confirms that it wishes to proceed and, if the Filer is still able to execute at the quoted price, the Client's market order at the quoted price will be filled by the Filer. If, upon the Client’s acceptance, the Filer is unable to execute the transaction at the quoted price, the order will be cancelled, the quoted price will be updated and the Client will be able to enter a new order to transact against the new price.
41. The Filer may also fill liquidity for Client orders using proprietary assets. In all cases, the Filer provides fair and reasonable pricing to Clients, including by considering prices available from the Filer’s Liquidity Providers and global benchmarks.
42. Clients can submit orders to the Filer in two ways: (i) a market order which specifies the desired trading pair and quantity; and (ii) a limit order (including, for clarity, stop orders) which specifies the desired trading pair, quantity and price at which the Client wishes to transact.
43. When a Client enters a limit order, the Filer will not process the trade until such future time as when the price from the Liquidity Provider plus the 'spread' meets the price entered by the client, and then the Client's order will automatically be executed.
44. For each Client limit order, the limit order may be partially or completely filled if the Client's specified limit price is met. If the market price plus the 'spread' does not meet the price specified in the limit order, the limit order remains open in the Client Account until it is cancelled by the client or filled. If the order remains open for 90 days, Clients are given a notification if they wish to cancel the order or keep it in place. If a limit order is partially filled, the rest of the order remains open in the Client Account. Open limit orders entered by Clients are displayed on the Platform; however, they are not available to trade against other Client orders.
45. The Filer promptly ensures that the increase or decrease in Crypto Assets in the Client’s Account resulting from the trade is reflected in the Crypto Asset balances held in custody on the Platform, as described below under “Custody of Crypto Assets.” To the extent necessary to fulfil its settlement obligations to Clients, the Filer may trade with its Liquidity Providers on a net basis.
46. Trading pairs available on the Platform include Crypto Asset-for-fiat and Crypto Asset-for-Crypto Asset.
47. Clients have access to a complete record of all transactions in their Client Account, including all incoming transfers of fiat or Crypto Assets, all purchases, sales and withdrawals, and the relevant prices, commissions and withdrawal fees charged in respect of such transactions.
48. Clients can fund their account by transferring in fiat currency or Crypto Assets. Clients can transfer in fiat currency by Interac e-transfer, bank wire, and other methods, with the minimum and maximum amount for each transfer type set out on the Platform. Interac e-transfers are subject to fees disclosed on the Platform and incorporated by reference into the Client Agreement. All transfers-in are initiated by the client and manually approved by the Filer prior to being accepted into the Client Account.
49. Clients that use the Filer’s custodial services may be charged a withdrawal fee when transferring Crypto Assets out of their Client Account to a blockchain address specified by the Client. This “on chain” withdrawal fee varies by Crypto Asset and the total withdrawal fee payable in respect of a withdrawal is disclosed prior to confirmation of withdrawal.
50. Prior to transferring Crypto Assets out of a Client Account, the Filer conducts secondary verification of the blockchain address and screens the blockchain address specified by the transferring Client using blockchain forensics software.
