51. The Filer’s books and records document all of the trades executed on the Platform. No order is accepted by the Filer unless there is sufficient cash or Crypto Assets available in the Client Account to complete the trade.
52. The Filer does not extend margin, credit, or other forms of leverage to Clients in connection with trading Crypto Contracts or Crypto Assets on the Platform, and does not offer derivatives based on Crypto Assets, other than Crypto Contracts.
53. The Filer promptly, and no later than two business days after the trade, settles transactions with the Liquidity Providers on a net basis. When there are net purchases of Crypto Assets with a Liquidity Provider, the Filer arranges for fiat to, and receipt of Crypto Assets from, the Liquidity Provider. When there are net sales of Crypto Assets, the Filer arranges for receipt of fiat from, and transfer of Crypto Assets to, the Liquidity Provider.
54. All fees and commissions earned by the Filer are clearly disclosed on the Platform, and the Filer’s Clients can check the quoted prices for Crypto Assets on the Platform against the prices available on other Registered CTPs in Canada and other public pricing sources.
55. Clients receive electronic trade confirmations and monthly statements setting out the details of the transaction history in their Client Account. Clients can view their transaction history and account balances in real time by accessing their Client Account using the Website or App.

73. The Filer is proficient and knowledgeable about staking Stakeable Crypto Assets.
74. The Filer itself does not act as a Validator. The Custodian and Validators are proficient and experienced in staking Stakeable Crypto Assets.
75. 77. The Filer, as part of its suitability assessment, evaluates whether offering the Staking Services is suitable for a Client before providing access to an account that makes available the Staking Services and, on an ongoing basis, at least once in each 12-month period.
78. The Filer only stakes the Stakeable Crypto Assets of those Clients who have agreed to the Staking Services and have allocated Stakeable Crypto Assets to be staked. Where a Client no longer wishes to stake all or a portion of the allocated Stakeable Crypto Assets, subject to any Lock-Up Periods (as defined below) or any terms of the Staking Services that permit the Client to remove Stakeable Crypto Assets from the Staking Services prior to the expiry of any Lock-Up Periods, the Filer ceases to stake those Stakeable Crypto Assets.
79. Before the first time a Client allocates any Stakeable Crypto Assets to be staked, the Filer delivers to the client the Risk Statement that includes the risks with respect to staking and the Staking Services described below, and requires the client to provide electronic acknowledgement of having received, read and understood the Risk Statement.
80. The Filer clearly explains in the Risk Statement the risks with respect to staking and the Staking Services in plain language.
81. The Filer stakes and unstakes Crypto Assets on an omnibus basis by calculating the total amount of a Stakeable Crypto Asset that clients wish to stake or unstake and adjusting the amount actually staked to reconcile with the net amount that clients have, in total, instructed the Filer to stake or unstake.
82. The Filer holds the staked Stakeable Crypto Assets in trust for or for the benefit of its clients in one or more omnibus Locations in the name of the Filer in trust for or for the benefit of the Filer's Clients with the Custodian separate and distinct from (i) the assets of the Filer, the Custodian and the Custodian's other clients; and (ii) the Crypto Assets held for its clients that have not agreed to staking those specific Crypto Assets. For greater certainty, the Filer (or the Custodians) will not stake Client Crypto Assets from the same Location in which it holds unstaked Client Crypto Assets.
83. The Filer and the Custodian remain in possession, custody and control of the staked Stakeable Crypto Assets at all times. At all times, the Custodian continues to hold the private keys or other cryptographic key material required to stake or unstake Clients' Stakeable Crypto Assets or to access staking rewards. Custody, possession and control of staked Stakeable Crypto Assets are not transferred to Validators or any other third parties in connection with the Staking Services.
84. The Filer has established and applies policies and procedures to address how staking rewards, fees and losses will be calculated and allocated to clients that have staked Stakeable Crypto Assets under the Staking Services.
85. Staking rewards are issued periodically and automatically by the blockchain protocol of the Stakeable Crypto Asset and received directly into the staking wallets with the Custodian. Other than any "validator commission" that may be received by a Validator under the rules of the blockchain protocol, Validators do not receive or otherwise have control over staking rewards earned by Clients.
86. Staking rewards are typically issued for a specific time period, often referred to as an "epoch". For each "epoch", the Filer promptly determines the amount of staking rewards earned by each Client that had staked Stakeable Crypto Assets under the Staking Services.
87. When staking rewards for a Stakeable Crypto Asset are received into staking wallets, the Filer promptly calculates the amount of the staking reward earned by each Client using the Staking Services in respect of that asset and credits each Client Account accordingly. Staking reward distributions are shown on the Platform and on Clients' account statements.
88. For certain Stakeable Crypto Assets, staking rewards are automatically staked by the blockchain protocol to compound rewards. Clients must unstake some or all of these rewards if they wish to sell or transfer them.
89. Where staking rewards are not compounded by the blockchain protocol, the Filer instructs the Custodian to transfer staking rewards from the staking wallets to other omnibus wallets holding Client Crypto Assets.
90. Certain Stakeable Crypto Assets are subject to a so-called "warm-up" or "bonding" period after being staked, during which time the Stakeable Crypto Assets do not earn any staking rewards. A client will not receive staking rewards in respect of any of their staked Stakeable Crypto Assets that are still subject to "warm-up" periods.
91. Similarly, a client will not receive staking rewards in respect of Stakeable Crypto Assets that have been unstaked by the Client but are still subject to Lock-up Periods.
92. The Filer does not promise or guarantee its Clients a specific staking reward rate for any Stakeable Crypto Asset. The Filer does not exercise any discretion to change reward rates.
93. The Filer may show on the Platform the current estimated reward rate for Stakeable Crypto Assets. This estimated reward rate is based on data derived from the blockchain for the Stakeable Crypto Asset and adjusted for any applicable validator commission or fees payable to the Filer.
94. The Filer charges a fee to clients using Staking Services based on a percentage of the Client's staking rewards. The Filer clearly discloses the fees charged by the Filer for the Staking Services and provides a clear calculation of the rewards earned by each Client that agrees to the Staking Services.
95. For certain Stakeable Crypto Assets, a Validator can, as part of the blockchain consensus protocol, set a percentage of the staking rewards earned by Stakeable Crypto Assets staked with the Validator to be received by the Validator. This is typically referred to as the "validator commission". The validator commission is deducted automatically by the underlying blockchain protocol from staking rewards and transferred by the protocol directly to the Validator. Where a "validator commission" applies, the Filer clearly discloses the existence and amount of the validator commission to Clients using the Staking Services.
96. Under the commercial agreements between the Filer and Validators, Validators may pay some of the validator commission to the Filer for arranging the staking of Clients' Stakeable Crypto Assets with the Validators. The Filer discloses to Clients that it receives a share of validator commissions. Further, the Filer has adopted policies and procedures for the selection of Validators and staking of Clients' Stakeable Crypto Assets to Validators to ensure that these decisions are based on factors other than the Filer's financial considerations under these commercial agreements.
97. For Stakeable Crypto Assets that do not have "validator commissions", the Filer pays a fee to the Validator and/or a Custodian for activating and operating nodes for the Filer's Clients using the Staking Services. This fee is included in the fee paid by Clients to the Filer in connection with the Staking Services.
98. Certain proof of stake blockchain protocols impose penalties where a validator fails to comply with protocol rules. This penalty is often referred to as "slashing" or "jailing". If a Validator is "slashed" or "jailed", a percentage of the tokens staked with that Validator and/or a percentage of staking rewards earned by Clients staking to that Validator is permanently lost and/or the Validator will not be selected to participate in transaction validation and any Stakeable Crypto Assets staked with that Validator will not be eligible to earn staking rewards. Accordingly, if a Validator fails to comply with protocol rules, a percentage of Crypto Assets staked or earned by the Filer's Clients may be lost (i.e., the balance of the staking wallet will be reduced automatically by the blockchain protocol) and/or the Filer's Clients will not earn staking rewards for a period of time.
99. For certain Stakeable Crypto Assets, the Filer may agree to reimburse Clients for slashing penalties. The Client Agreement clearly provides for the circumstances the Filer will provide this reimbursement in respect of a Stakeable Crypto Asset. The availability of any reimbursement, and any conditions or limits on the reimbursement, are also described in the Risk Statement or the relevant Crypto Asset Statement.
100.To mitigate the risk of slashing or jailing to clients, the Filer may, where feasible, arrange to stake Stakeable Crypto Assets across multiple Validators, so that any penalty resulting from the actions or inaction of a specific Validator does not affect all staked Crypto Assets and the Filer can, if appropriate, re-stake with alternative Validators.
101.In addition, the Filer monitors its Validators for, among other things, downtime, jailing and slashing events and takes any appropriate action to protect Stakeable Crypto Assets staked by Clients.

Visa’s Stablecoin Platform: How VSP Could Redefine Institutional Payments ACI Information Group
Market Context
Stablecoin Growth: According to the Stablecoin Market Outlook 2026 by MarketsandMarkets, the global stablecoin market is projected to grow from USD 14 billion in 2024 to USD 48 billion by 2029, driven primarily by cross‑border remittances, treasury optimization, and decentralized finance (DeFi) integrations.
Regulatory Momentum: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Federal Reserve have increased enforcement actions against unregistered stablecoin issuers. The European Banking Authority’s Digital Asset Regulation 2025 framework introduces “regulatory sandbox” provisions that could facilitate compliant deployment of institutional‑grade stablecoins.
Competitive Landscape: Established payment networks (Mastercard, American Express) and fintech incumbents (Stripe, Square) are launching parallel stablecoin offerings. Meanwhile, crypto-native platforms such as Coinbase and Circle are pursuing institutional APIs that bypass traditional banking intermediaries.
These dynamics set the stage for Visa’s entry into a crowded yet lucrative segment where institutional trust, regulatory compliance, and operational security are paramount.
Product Overview
Feature Description Strategic Implication
Single Environment for Mint, Redeem, Hold, Transfer Visa‑managed sandbox that hosts OUSD and future stablecoins Reduces integration friction for issuers; lowers technical barrier to entry
Wallet‑as‑a‑Service (WaaS) On‑chain wallet infrastructure with secure passkeys and audit trails Enhances security posture and aligns with compliance frameworks
Dual‑Approval Workflows & Transfer Allow Lists Multi‑signer approvals and whitelisted counterparties Meets Know‑Your‑Customer (KYC) and Anti‑Money Laundering (AML) standards
Audit Logging & Secure Passkeys Immutable transaction records and hardware‑backed authentication Facilitates regulatory reporting and audit readiness
The platform’s architecture suggests a deliberate attempt to align stablecoin operations with Visa’s existing payment, treasury, and fraud‑management services. By enabling stablecoin flows within familiar payment pipelines, VSP could accelerate institutional adoption for use cases such as cross‑border remittance, treasury hedging, and programmable settlement.
Business Fundamentals
Revenue Streams
Transaction Fees: Per‑transaction fees on stablecoin minting, redemption, and transfer. Early estimates suggest a fee structure comparable to Visa’s traditional interchange rates (0.3 %–0.5 %).
Subscription Model: Annual licensing for WaaS and compliance tooling, projected at USD 2.5 million for mid‑tier issuers.
Value‑Added Services: Integration with Visa’s Treasury Management Suite and Fraud Detection APIs, potentially generating upsell opportunities.
Cost Structure
Infrastructure: Cloud hosting, on‑chain node maintenance, and security tooling. Initial beta phase costs are estimated at USD 1.2 million per annum.
Regulatory & Compliance: Ongoing legal counsel, audit services, and KYC/AML certifications. Annual compliance spend projected at USD 500 k for the beta cohort.
Marketing & Partnerships: Partnerships with stablecoin issuers and fintech accelerators; projected marketing spend of USD 750 k.
Financial Projections Assuming a conservative penetration of 25 % of the 2,000 institutional issuers identified in the Institutional Stablecoin Survey 2025, VSP could capture USD 40 million in revenue in year two, with EBITDA margins of 35 % after scaling.
Regulatory Landscape
Jurisdiction Key Regulations Impact on VSP
United States SEC’s Unregistered Securities Act, FinCEN’s AML Regulations VSP’s dual‑approval workflow satisfies KYC/AML; however, issuers must register as “money services businesses” (MSBs) if they hold customer funds.
European Union MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets) Requires a European Banking Authority license; VSP’s compliance tooling must be updated to align with MiCA’s transparency and capital requirements.
Asia Pacific Singapore Monetary Authority’s Digital Payment Token (DPT) Guidelines Enables VSP’s “stablecoin‑as‑a‑service” model; issuers can register as “digital token issuers” with lower capital thresholds.
Visa’s strong regulatory track record and its existing network of compliance experts provide an advantage, but the fragmented regulatory environment across jurisdictions introduces operational complexity and potential legal exposure.
Competitive Dynamics
Legacy Payment Networks: Mastercard’s Mosaic and American Express’s Pay with Amex are launching stablecoin APIs that mirror VSP’s architecture but lack a dedicated WaaS component. Visa’s advantage lies in its deep integration with payment processing and fraud detection.
Fintech Leaders: Stripe’s Stablecoin Connect and Square’s Issuer Platform prioritize API simplicity, offering “pay‑as‑you‑go” pricing models. VSP’s subscription approach may deter price‑sensitive issuers.
Crypto‑Native Platforms: Coinbase’s Issuer API provides end‑to‑end stablecoin solutions but operates on a decentralized infrastructure that may appeal to issuers prioritizing decentralization over the centralized security Visa offers.
The differentiation hinges on Visa’s promise of a unified, secure environment that reduces the operational burden on issuers—a compelling proposition for conservative institutions.
Risks & Opportunities
Category Risk Opportunity
Technical Integration Legacy systems may struggle with on‑chain wallet integration, leading to delays. Visa’s WaaS component could reduce integration time, capturing early adopters who value speed.
Regulatory Uncertainty Sudden regulatory tightening (e.g., MiCA’s capital requirements) could raise entry barriers. Visa’s compliance infrastructure could allow rapid adaptation, positioning it as the go‑to platform for compliant issuers.
Market Adoption Institutional inertia and preference for existing fiat settlement may slow uptake. Stablecoins enable near‑real‑time settlement and lower cross‑border fees, offering a competitive edge for banks seeking cost efficiencies.
Competitive Pressures Fintechs may offer lower fees or more flexible APIs. Visa’s brand trust and network effects can justify premium pricing for high‑volume issuers.
Operational Security Misconfiguration of dual‑approval workflows could expose issuers to fraud. Visa’s audit logging and secure passkeys can be marketed as industry‑leading security standards.
The balance between these factors will determine whether VSP becomes a mainstream institutional tool or remains a niche offering for a small subset of crypto‑savvy issuers.
Market Impact
If VSP successfully integrates stablecoin operations into traditional payment flows, it could accelerate the convergence of fiat and digital assets across the global financial system. Potential ripple effects include:
Reduced Settlement Times: Near-instantaneous stablecoin transfers could lower the cost of cross‑border remittances.
Treasury Efficiency: Institutions could hold a digital dollar reserve that is fully interoperable with global payment networks.
Competitive Disruption: Traditional banks may need to adopt similar platforms to remain competitive with fintechs that already offer stablecoin‑enabled services.
Conclusion
Visa’s launch of the Stablecoin Platform signals a deliberate effort to capitalize on the burgeoning institutional demand for programmable money while leveraging its entrenched payment infrastructure. The platform’s comprehensive security and compliance features address key institutional pain points, and the financial projections suggest a viable revenue stream if adoption targets are met. However, the fragmented regulatory environment, fierce competition from both legacy payment providers and fintech disruptors, and potential operational integration challenges represent significant hurdles. Only through sustained beta testing, regulatory alignment, and value‑driven pricing will VSP be able to secure a lasting foothold in the evolving stablecoin ecosystem.

Coinbase admits trust gap as Base faces crypto backlash ACI Information Group
The controversy regarding Base’s loss of credibility in the crypto community has now moved into the higher levels of Coinbase, creating doubts that go beyond social media. This controversy is important because today Base isn’t just another layer-2 blockchain anymore. Now it is processing more of the onchain stablecoin volume than any other blockchain and is also securing $11.61 billion in total value, as per L2BEAT, thus making it one of the main infrastructure pieces of the industry.
The conversation took place on X on July 18, after a crypto trader named Rune (@RuneCrypto_) had a chat with Cobie, who has just assumed the lead of the Coinbase Base application, regarding the reasons why users should pick the application. Cobie responded to Rune’s key concern that Coinbase has often been “a little bit in an ivory tower and a little bit distant from users,” especially those who are into crypto-centric businesses.
Coinbase admits trust gap
Coinbase’s admission marks a major transformation in the company, which recently reported a record high of 8.6% of the total crypto trading volume in the world as of Q1 2026. By admitting the gap between them and the users driving onchain adoption, the company is trying to win back the trust of the crypto sector.
Jesse Pollak is still in charge of the operations of the Base network. On July 16, Pollak announced that he would be handing the consumer app over to Cobie, so that he could focus on Base, which he calls the biggest chance ever to build a blockchain for the global financial system.
The change in leadership came after a difficult quarter. Just a day earlier, Pollak had remarked that the quarter had been “a punch in the face” and had unveiled his plans for the company, which would entail trading, a payment function, and AI agents. Moreover, he has acknowledged that Base is not successful in its foray into social apps and thus the project will now be focusing on its other activities which have potential in the longer run.
Armstrong already conceded the misstep
Brian Armstrong, the chief executive officer of Coinbase, admitted that the organization has made a mistake before the latest developments.
Armstrong talked about the failure of the “content coins” project of Base on July 13, saying, “We have messed up, time to turn the page.” According to him, the company shifted the focus away from the project at the beginning of the year and now prioritizes trade, payments, and AI agents.
His remarks mirrored Pollak’s assessment and seemed to indicate that Coinbase executives are united in their desire to move past the previous strategy based on social media. But whether this reset will lead to renewed confidence will depend more on execution than on public relations.
Why the dispute matters
For the larger cryptocurrency market, what is more important is how Base is growing as a player in on-chain finance. In its Q1 2026 letter to shareholders, Coinbase noted that Base handled 62% of the global on-chain stablecoin transaction volume–more than the total volume of all other blockchains together. The firm also said that Base processed above 90% of the global on-chain stablecoin volume with regard to agentic stablecoins, while the volume of stablecoin trades on Base grew tenfold compared to the previous year.
The mentioned numbers make Base one of the key settlement layers in the industry. A blockchain with such a huge volume of stablecoin transactions benefits from the confidence of developers, liquidity providers, and crypto-savvy users responsible for creating applications and transferring money in the networks. Any evidence of lack of trust in Base would have an impact beyond the limits of Coinbase.
Additionally, the discussion takes place while Base is dealing with another technical milestone. Currently, L2BEAT credits the network with the designation of a Stage 1 optimistic rollup, although it is likely to come down to Stage 0 in roughly 30 days due to its proof system not complying with the upcoming trusted-setup requirements.
While the governance review is not connected to the public row, they do raise the same issue of whether Base is capable of enhancing its technical roadmaps as well as the ties with the cryptocurrency community as it develops further. In the next days, we will be able to see whether Coinbase’s new approach towards crypto-native clients brings about certain product improvements and whether the anticipated L2BEAT reclassification proceeds as expected.

Used Nissan Ariya (Mk1, 2021-date) buyer's guide: low prices make EV even more appealing Richard Dredge Autovia
Verdict
It takes something special to bag our Car of the Year award, but that’s what the Nissan Ariya did in 2022, also claiming the Best Mid-sized Company Car trophy in the process. We were impressed with the Nissan’s blend of good looks, high-quality cabin and decent range. But that was then and the EV world is fast-paced, so although there’s no doubt that the Ariya is still a very good car, its so-so real-world efficiency, relatively small boot capacity and lacklustre driving experience  mean it’s overshadowed by some rivals. Don’t be too quick to dismiss the Ariya though, because it still has a lot to offer, and if you can buy one at the right price, you can forgive its shortcomings.
Nissan was the first company to unveil an affordable electric car with the Leaf. That was in 2010, just as SUV mania was starting to take a hold, so it seems incredible that it took the brand another decade to introduce an electric SUV, which it did in 2020 with the Ariya, having shown a concept the year before.
Sadly for Nissan, while the original Leaf had no competition when it arrived, by the time the Ariya went on sale, the segment was already getting busy, and since then it has only got busier. As a result, while the Ariya is a really good family car with a lot to offer, it’s up against rivals that can eclipse the in some respects.
Which one should I buy?
The Ariya typically gets through electricity at the rate of 2.9 miles per kWh – or just 2.5 miles in the winter – and motorway driving will bring that down even further.
Depending on how you use your car, the 63kWh battery might be sufficient, but an 87kWh model will provide greater peace of mind; all Ariyas can charge at up to 130kW. Buy an 87kWh Ariya and the less powerful (314bhp) motor is all you need, and even Engage models are pretty well equipped. These have all-LED exterior lighting, front and rear parking sensors and a rear camera, a heat pump, ambient cabin lighting and navigation.

Advance trim adds a hands-free powered tailgate, heating for the steering wheel, front seats and windscreen, synthetic leather
trim, wireless phone charging, a 360-degree camera and extra driver-assistance systems. The Evolve has an opening panoramic glass roof, ventilated front seats, heated rear seats and a Bose hi-fi.
Prices
Advance is the most popular Ariya trim level, followed by Evolve; relatively few of the cars for sale are Engage editions. You can buy a used Nissan Ariya for less than £15,000 through our Buy a Car service, while a used Nissan Ariya Nismo is available for around £32,000.
Check the price of a used Nissan Ariya with our free car valuation tool...
On the road
If you’re a keen driver, you’ll be disappointed by the lack of engagement – there’s not a lot of feel to many of the Ariya’s controls. Even the Nismo version isn’t as much fun to drive as it should be, because you can really feel the car’s 2.2-ton weight. But the Ariya shrugs off broken road surfaces far more readily than many cars in this segment, and refinement is excellent at motorway speeds.
There’s also masses of grip, so in adverse conditions the Ariya feels reassuring, much helped by impressive high-speed stability and, on e-4ORCE models, the fitment of four-wheel drive.
Alternatives to the Nissan Ariya
The mid-sized electric SUV class is booming, partly thanks to an influx of cars from China. Among these are the Xpeng G6, BYD Sealion 7 and MG S6, while the European offerings include the Peugeot E-5008 and its cousins, the DS 7 E-Tense, Citroen e-C5 Aircross and Vauxhall Grandland Electric.
Ford and VW each provide two options: the Mustang-Mach-E and the Explorer for the former, and the ID.4 and ID.5 for the latter. Also within the Volkswagen Group are the Skoda Enyaq and Cupra Tavascan, while your shortlist should also include the Tesla
Model Y, Toyota bZ4X, Kia EV6 and Hyundai Ioniq 5, along with the Volvo EC40 and EX40.
What to look for
Feeling flat
The 12-volt battery can go flat very quickly, while premature failure of it is another common problem. Some owners have resorted to carrying a booster pack with them, just in case their car lets them down.
On the pull
If you’re buying an Ariya to tow with it, be sure to go for one of the all-wheel-drive e-4ORCE models. These are rated to pull up to 1,500kg whereas the front-wheel-drive editions are limited to just 750kg.
Other glitches
Fast charging can result in the car locking up altogether, with permanent fixes sometimes hard to come by. Driver- assistance systems and the infotainment crashing can result from outdated software.
Range requirements
Nissan claimed a range of 250 miles for 63kWh models, and 314-329 miles for 87kWh cars depending on power and trim. We averaged 230 miles when we ran an 87kWh e-4ORCE model on our test fleet.
Interior
Showing just how quickly cutting-edge tech can date, the Ariya’s digital displays are already looking a little passé. However, the cabin quality still impresses, and the touch-sensitive controls work well. Rear-seat space is good, but the pay-off is a relatively small boot that can hold just 466-1,350 litres (408-1,280 litres in e-4ORCE models).
Running costs
The service interval is set at 12 months or 10,000 miles. Services alternate between Minor and Major at £190 and £250; the latter includes fresh brake fluid every two years, and each service comes with a year’s worth of RAC breakdown cover. To help spread the cost of maintenance, all Nissan dealers offer customers a monthly payment plan.
Insurance groups range from 30 to 41, although the highest is for the Nismo as well as the various e-4ORCE models; the bulk of the cars for sale are in groups 31-34. Until its sixth birthday, any Ariya that cost more than £50,000 new (including any factory-fitted options) is liable for the £440 expensive car road tax supplement. Most, but not all, 87kWh models breached the £50k mark, so it’s worth establishing how much road tax you’ll have to pay before buying.
Recalls
There have been four recalls so far. Nissan issued the first in May 2023, for cars built between April and August 2022, which could suffer from instrumentation glitches; an over-the-air software update fixed things. The next campaign came in October 2023, because some cars manufactured between March 2022 and April 2023 suffered from short circuits in the electric motors; once again a software update fixed the problem.
Recall three came in August 2024, because of faulty oil seals fitted to some Ariyas that were produced between May 2022 and June 2023. A new traction motor was the solution. Lastly, some Ariyas built between March 2022 and February 2025 left the factory with incorrectly aligned headlights; they were recalled in November 2025.
Driver Power owner satisfaction
The Ariya isn’t a big seller in the UK – although there are plenty for sale – so it has never appeared in a Driver Power survey. Nissan has appeared in our Brands survey though, and in 2025 it came 15th out of 31, having come done exactly the same thing in 2024.
There’s just one owner review on Carbuyer.co.uk; they awarded their Ariya three stars out of five because while they really liked
it when it was working, on too many occasions it was in the workshop being fixed.

Sadly for Nissan, while the original Leaf had no competition when it arrived, by the time the Ariya went on sale, the segment was already getting busy, and since then it has only got busier. As a result, while the Ariya is a really good family car with a lot to offer, it’s up against rivals that can eclipse the Nissan in some respects.
History
The Ariya was unveiled in July 2020, but it didn’t go on sale in the UK until December 2021. There were two trim levels (Advance and Evolve), both available with three different powertrains. Entry-level cars came with 214bhp, a 63kWh battery and front-wheel drive, while mid-range models had 238bhp, an 87kWh battery and front-wheel drive. The range-topping e-4ORCE had 301bhp, an 87kWh battery and all-wheel drive.
In August 2023 a new entry-level trim, Engage, was introduced for the front-wheel-drive models and at the top of the range there was a new 388bhp edition called the e-4ORCE Evolve+. In October 2024 a 429bhp Nismo option joined the range with a sportier chassis set-up, bodykit and upgraded interior.
An updated Ariya is arriving imminently, with a refreshed exterior design, recalibrated suspension, extra colour options and improved charging.

headline: I tested iOS 26 Siri against iOS 27 Siri AI in my car - and it wasn't even close
detail_text:
I tested iOS 26 Siri against iOS 27 Siri AI in my car - and it wasn't even close
Matched:
AAPL
Source: Indian Technology News
Publication Date: 7/21/2026 6:50:49 AM
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google. As an iPhone user, I often get frustrated with Siri's inability to correctly respond to my questions and requests. That's especially true in the car when I'm driving.
I tested iOS 26 Siri against iOS 27 Siri AI in my car - and it wasn't even close Omniearth
Follow ZDNET: Add us as a preferred source on Google.
As an iPhone user, I often get frustrated with Siri's inability to correctly respond to my questions and requests. That's especially true in the car when I'm driving. And when it fails to respond or gives me the wrong answer, that's a distraction I don't need when I'm behind the wheel.
That's why I've been looking forward to the new Siri AI, due to officially roll out in September with iOS 27. This latest generation of the voice assistant promises to be more responsive, more accurate, and less frustrating.
Does Siri AI live up to the hype? To answer that question, I recently took two iPhones with me in the car -- one with iOS 26 and the other with the iOS 27 public beta. I tasked both of them with the same questions and requests to see if and how the new Siri bested the current flavor. Here's what happened.
If you want to try out the new Siri as well, here's what you'll need.
Now, here are some of the questions and requests I gave to both versions of Siri, and how each responded.
For this test, I asked Siri to give me directions to a doctor listed among my contacts. I simply told it to take me to Dr. [person's last name]. Regular Siri didn't even seem to consult my contacts and instead gave me a list of doctors on the web, none of whom matched the right one.
In contrast, Siri AI clearly scanned my contacts and immediately gave me directions to the correct doctor.
Winner: Siri AI
Here, I asked Siri for driving directions. Both regular Siri and Siri AI complied with my request. But then I started a new conversation and asked each to avoid toll roads. Siri AI changed the existing directions based on my new request. But regular Siri just gave me generic information on how to avoid toll roads.
This test was less about driving directions and more about Siri's ability to connect a new conversation or request to a previous one.
Both regular Siri and Siri AI were able to find local restaurants based on specific cuisines. But they differed in their responses to follow-up questions. After each displayed the list of restaurants I requested, I asked both to give me the ratings and reviews for each one.
Siri had trouble with this request as it sometimes described a different set of restaurants based on their reviews. But Siri AI nailed this each time by providing the requested details for the restaurants on the screen.
For this test, I asked both editions of Siri to tell me something interesting about the town I was driving through. Regular Siri told me I could search the web for that when I finished driving. In contrast, Siri AI served up some interesting facts about the current town.
For this one, I asked both flavors of Siri to play some Beatles music. By default, regular Siri tuned up the Beatles channel on Sirius XM even though I didn't specify that as the source. I even asked it to play Beatles songs from my own music library, and still it turned to Sirius XM. When I asked Siri AI to play Beatles music, it automatically grabbed the tunes from my library.
Siri AI is designed to respond to multi-part requests, a more complex type of task that regular Siri can't handle. This means you can bundle several tasks in one shot.
Here, I asked it to find a recipe for lentil soup on the internet, create a shopping list of the ingredients, and text me the list. It followed each step correctly, ending with the list of items texted to me.
Both versions of Siri can provide certain kinds of general information. But Siri AI is better equipped for the task. Depending on the question, regular Siri may simply give up, tell you to check the web later when you're not driving, or turn over the job to ChatGPT. In contrast, Siri AI was able to answer all the questions I threw at it, and more adeptly.
As one example, I asked both flavors of Siri to explain Einstein's special theory of relativity. Regular Siri provided a brief answer grabbed from a single source on the web. Siri AI served up more details pulled from several different web sources and organized them all into one cohesive explanation. It then suggested a couple of sub-topics and asked me which one I'd like to explore.
I asked both flavors of Siri to tell me a story. When I didn't specify the topic, both told me a brief tale, though the one from Siri AI was more clever and creative. Then I specified a topic, asking each to tell me a story about my cat, Mr. Giggles, traveling to the moon.
Regular Siri told me it couldn't do that while I was in the car and that I'd have to do it on my iPhone. Siri AI kicked off an entertaining story about my favorite cat.
Here, I asked each version of Siri to play a game. Regular Siri told me I'd have to open an app for that. Siri AI was ready to challenge me with a game, though its options were limited to flipping a coin, drawing a card, rolling some dice, or playing Rock, Paper, and Scissors. When I asked it to play a trivia game about American history, it told me it couldn't do that.
This does point out a key aspect of Siri AI. It's purposely designed to be less entertaining and more serious than other AIs such as ChatGPT and Gemini. That's not a bad thing, but I would like to see it develop a bit of a playful side as well.
Finally, I asked Siri to teach me a language. Regular Siri said it could search the web for that when I've finished driving. Siri AI asked me what language I wanted to learn, and I mentioned Italian. It then offered me basic, conversational phrases in both Italian and English, explained what each one meant, and continued the lesson by giving me more words and phrases.
Siri AI clearly was the winner, at least when it came to more complex and nuanced tasks. Did it score each time? No, not quite.
Sometimes it didn't let me finish my end of the conversation, especially when I was trying to give it a multi-part request. Other times it would simply fail to respond and then time out. But as Siri AI is still in beta mode at this point, it's naturally going to have some rough edges. Hopefully, the new Siri will be fine-tuned by the time it makes its official debut in September.
First, you have to grab the iOS 27 public beta. Beyond being compatible with this version of the OS, your phone must also support Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. That means you need an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, any iPhone 16 model, or any iPhone 17 model. Since even the first public beta could be unstable, avoid installing it on your primary phone. Instead, use a spare or test iPhone. I'm using a spare iPhone 15 Pro.
Second, you need access to Siri AI. With the developer beta of iOS 27, you had to join a waitlist and be patient. With the public beta, there's no more waitlist, so you can dive right in.
Third, your iPhone must be connected and set up in your car through Apple CarPlay. The specific steps can vary slightly based on the make of your vehicle. But this Apple support article should help you with the process if you're not already set up.
To cut to the chase, how did Siri AI and regular Siri compare and contrast with each other? When I gave them simple requests such as asking for driving directions to a specific address, texting or calling someone, checking my calendar, and adding a reminder, they both fared about the same. But when I ramped up the challenge by posing more complex questions, Siri AI then proved its worth.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 prices leaked ahead of Launch Omniearth
July 21 --
Samsung's big Unpacked event is just a day away, but it looks like the pricing surprise came early. A fresh leak out of Europe suggests the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 are set to cost noticeably more than their predecessors, and that's got a lot of people wondering whether India will get hit with the same hike. Between these new leaks and the way things have been trending lately, it's starting to look like last year's prices might not survive this generation.
What the European leak actually shows
The numbers came from a Portuguese retailer that apparently published its product listings a bit too early. Worth noting: Portugal slaps a 23% VAT on electronics, so the prices there tend to run higher than elsewhere in Europe, which is something to keep in mind before assuming these figures apply everywhere.
Still, a price bump wouldn't exactly come out of nowhere. Samsung's already raised prices on several fronts in India this year - its Galaxy Tab S lineup saw increases recently, and even the Galaxy M47, which had only just launched, got a price adjustment within days of hitting shelves.
And Samsung isn't the only one doing this. Apple, OnePlus, Nothing, and Realme have all increased their prices upward in recent months too, largely thanks to rising component costs. Given that pattern, it'd honestly be a bit surprising if the Fold 8 stuck to last year's price tag.
The same leaked listing also gave a glimpse at Samsung's upcoming wearables. The Galaxy Watch 9 is tipped to start at about ₹45,000 for the 40mm Bluetooth version, with the 44mm model coming in at roughly ₹48,000 - add around ₹5500 more if you want LTE. The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, meanwhile, is expected to launch at approximately ₹83,000.
According to the listing, the Z Flip 8 will still come in two storage flavours - 256GB and 512GB - priced at about ₹1,48,000 and around ₹1,71,000. The Z Fold 8, meanwhile, is expected to offer three tiers: 256GB, 512GB, and a 1TB option. Pricing reportedly starts at roughly ₹2,28,000, climbs to around ₹2,50,000 for the mid-tier, and tops out at about ₹2,94,000 for the 1TB model.
There's also chatter about Samsung finally bringing out an "Ultra" version of the Fold. If the leaked info holds up, that model could cost around ₹22,000 more than the standard Fold 8 - no matter which storage size you go with.
What does this mean for India?
Nothing is confirmed yet on the Indian pricing front, but the signs aren't exactly reassuring. The Galaxy Z Fold 7 launched here at ₹1,74,999 for the base 12GB+256GB model, and if the European increases are any indication, the Fold 8 could edge closer to the ₹2,00,000 mark this time around.
That said, it's worth being cautious about reading too much into the European numbers directly - pricing in Europe is almost always higher than in India thanks to differences in taxation, so a straight conversion isn't a reliable way to predict the actual Indian price.

University of Portsmouth celebrates inspirational figures with Honorary Doctorates at 2026 graduation National World plc
The University of Portsmouth has announced nine extraordinary individuals will receive Honorary Doctorates and Honorary Fellowships during its 2026 graduation ceremonies this month.
The first two recipients - comedian Suzi Ruffell and music industry strategist Joshua Robinson - receive their awards today (21 July) at the Guildhall, marking the start of two weeks of celebrations for thousands of graduating students.
This year's recipients represent a diverse range of achievement across comedy, entertainment, maritime, business, music, humanitarian work, science, technology and sport, embodying the University's values of excellence, innovation and community impact.
High-profile figures include:
Portsmouth-based comedian Suzi Ruffell, known for her sell-out stand-up tours and hit podcasts including Out With Suzi Ruffell and Big Kick Energy
Music industry strategist Joshua Robinson, who founded the RecFest festival while studying at the University of Portsmouth’s Business School and still bases his office at Portsmouth Guildhall
Dr Shahriar Hossain, a member of the Revolution Plastics Institute Advisory Council and internationally recognised environmental campaigner who helped make Bangladesh the first country to ban plastic shopping bags
Master Mariner Captain Philippa Bowden MNM, who grew up in the city before a career navigating some of the world's most remote polar waters
Nadia Huma Arab, a Portsmouth entrepreneur whose acclaimed cookbook, The Road From Karachi, funds clean water pumps worldwide
Honorary Doctorates and Fellowships are the highest accolades the University can give, recognising exceptional achievement and outstanding contribution to society. Previous Portsmouth recipients include Sabrina Dhowre Elba, Tim Campbell MBE and Alice Hendy MBE, honoured in 2025, and astronaut Tim Peake, physicist and broadcaster Professor Jim Al-Khalili and sailing legend Sir Ben Ainslie in earlier years, reflecting the University's long tradition of recognising excellence across business, science, the arts and public life.
Vice-Chancellor Professor Graham Galbraith CBE said: “Every year I am struck by the breadth of talent and generosity of spirit among our honorary graduates, and this year is no exception. From the world of comedy and broadcasting to maritime exploration, science and humanitarian work, this year's recipients show what is possible when ability is matched with purpose. It is particularly special to celebrate individuals with such deep connections to Portsmouth, whose achievements reflect the very best of our University and our city.”
Friends and family unable to attend the University of Portsmouth graduation ceremonies in person can watch live online at www.port.ac.uk/student-life/graduation.
If you would like to nominate an individual for an Honorary Doctorate next year, please visit www.port.ac.uk/form/honorary-degree-awards.
2026 Honorary Doctorate and Fellowship recipients
Suzi Ruffell - Comedian and Podcaster (Honorary Doctorate)
With five sell-out runs at the Edinburgh Fringe and a nomination for Best Stand-Up Show at the National Comedy Awards, Suzi Ruffell has become one of the country's most in-demand comedians, appearing on Live at the Apollo, Mock the Week and The Jonathan Ross Show. She co-hosts the podcasts Like Minded Friends and OUT With Suzi Ruffell, celebrating LGBT+ lives, as well as the smash-hit Big Kick Energy with fellow comedian Maisie Adam. Her debut book, Am I Having Fun Now?, became an instant Sunday Times bestseller in June 2025, and she is currently touring her latest stand-up show, The Juggle.
Joshua Robinson - Music Industry Strategist (Honorary Fellowship)
Music industry strategist and presenter Josh Robinson has spent over a decade championing emerging artists and transforming how musicians build sustainable careers. He studied at the University of Portsmouth's Business School, where he founded RecFest, a live music and entertainment festival rooted in Hampshire that has grown into a celebrated platform for rising talent. Josh leads LMSUK, home to a roster of 150 global artists, and is widely sought after for his expertise in musician social media strategy. His office remains at Portsmouth Guildhall, reflecting his enduring commitment to the city that shaped him.
Read Josh's full profile at port.ac.uk
Captain Philippa Bowden MNM - Master Mariner and Ice Navigator (Honorary Doctorate)
Captain Philippa Ann Bowden MNM is an Unlimited Master Mariner, ice navigator and maritime educator who spent her formative years in Portsmouth before entering the Merchant Navy at the age of nineteen. Her career spans cargo, research and passenger vessels, culminating in commanding expedition ships to remote destinations worldwide, with a specialism in polar regions. She delivers advanced maritime simulation training and mentors international female mariners, and was awarded the Merchant Navy Medal for Meritorious Service in 2025 for her outstanding contribution to maritime education and safety.
Joe Wells - Comedian, Author and Neurodiversity Advocate (Honorary Fellowship)
Joe Wells's writing career began at 15 with his first book, Touch and Go Joe, about his experience of OCD. Since then he has built a career as a stand-up comedian, writer and podcaster whose work explores neurodiversity, mental health and his own autistic identity; The Guardian has described his material as among the most thought-provoking coming from any comedian working today. In 2020, his stand-up clip on having a non-autistic brother went viral, gaining over 4.5 million views, and he now has an online following of more than 150,000. He co-hosts the Neurodivergent Moments podcast, and his book of the same name was published in 2026 to glowing reviews.
David Willan - Business Leader and Former Chair of the Board of Governors (Honorary Doctorate)
Born in Gosport, David Willan is Portsmouth through and through. A marketing consultant by profession, he has set up, developed, led and sold businesses specialising in research, planning and strategy consulting, including BPRI, winner of the Queen's Award for Enterprise. At the University of Portsmouth he chairs the Revolution Plastics Institute Advisory Council and served as a governor for nine years, including as Chair of the Board of Governors, helping guide the University through the Covid-19 pandemic, Brexit and a long-term freeze in tuition fees. A lifelong Pompey fan and former director of Portsmouth Football Club, he was instrumental in building the partnership between the club and the University.
Read David's full profile at port.ac.uk
Dr Tevin Tobun - Business Leader, Entrepreneur and Philanthropist (Honorary Doctorate)
Tevin Tobun is a business leader, entrepreneur and philanthropist with more than two decades of experience in technology, logistics and innovation. He founded Routd, a logistics technology platform, and the multi-award-winning GV Group, one of the UK's leading logistics and distribution companies; through businesses including Platebox and Repco Global, his enterprises distribute goods worth more than £400 million annually, including over 25 million school meals each year. He founded The Tobun Foundation to support young people from disadvantaged backgrounds into higher education and meaningful careers, and serves on the Lloyds Bank Business Advisory Board and as a Council member of The Open University.
Nadia Huma Arab - Entrepreneur and Humanitarian (Honorary Fellowship)
Portsmouth entrepreneur Nadia Arab blends cultural heritage, innovation and global humanitarian impact. Her acclaimed cookbook, The Road From Karachi, developed over four and a half years and rooted in her mother's lost recipes, is now taught in schools and stocked in Waitrose Southsea and Waterstones. Proceeds fund clean water pumps worldwide – more than 177 installed across India, Pakistan, Nepal, Gaza, Sri Lanka and Kenya, over 100 of them carrying the Portsmouth crest. Also, an IT lecturer at HSDC and a fitness trainer, Nadia's story has reached national audiences through the BBC's The Repair Shop, and she received the Inspirational Woman of Portsmouth Award in 2025 and an outstanding Humanitarian Award in 2026.
Dr Anne-Marie Imafidon MBE – Mathematician, Computer Scientist and STEM Advocate (Honorary Doctorate)
A trailblazing mathematician and computer scientist, Dr Anne-Marie Imafidon MBE became the youngest girl ever to pass A-level computing at just 11, later earning a Master's degree in Mathematics and Computer Science from the University of Oxford at 20. Her career has included roles at Goldman Sachs, Hewlett-Packard and Deutsche Bank, and she has held influential positions including Chair of the Institute for the Future of Work, President of the British Science Association and Women in Tech Envoy for the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. She is widely recognised as co-founder of Stemettes, the award-winning social enterprise that has inspired over 70,000 young people across Europe to pursue STEM.
Professor Dr Shahriar Hossain – Environmental Scientist and Plastic Pollution Campaigner (Honorary Doctorate)
Dr Shahriar Hossain, a member of the Revolution Plastics Institute Advisory Council, is an internationally recognised environmental advocate and public health campaigner who has spent more than 30 years protecting people and the environment from pollution and hazardous chemicals. As founder and Secretary General of Bangladesh's Environment and Social Development Organization (ESDO), he helped lead the campaign that made Bangladesh the first country in the world to ban plastic shopping bags, inspiring action worldwide. He has also played a leading role in international efforts to tackle toxic chemicals and mercury pollution, advised governments and global organisations, and currently serves as a negotiator for the Government of Bangladesh in the Global Plastics Treaty talks. His contributions to environmental protection have been recognised through numerous international honours, including the United Nations Environment Programme's Global 500 Roll of Honour.

iPhone 18 Pro Launch Date Tipped, Key Specifications Leak Hint At Major Camera Upgrades Omniearth
July 21 --
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro appears to be inching closer to its expected September unveiling, with a fresh round of analysis pointing to an exact keynote date, while separate leaks suggest the new flagship could bring one of the biggest camera overhauls in recent iPhone history alongside a next generation processor.
iPhone 18 Pro series keynote date narrowed down to September 9
Forbes has laid out a detailed case for when Apple will hold its annual iPhone event this year, based on the company's own scheduling history. Every iPhone keynote since 2012 has fallen between September 7 and September 14, with the sole exception being 2020, when the event was pushed to September 15 due to the pandemic. Apple has also never held the keynote on September 11 or on the day immediately after Labor Day, and has never scheduled it before the holiday either.
According to a report by the Sunday Guardian, the devices are tipped to feature a new variable aperture main camera paired with a Sony IMX905 sensor, marking what could be the biggest imaging upgrade to the lineup in years. The report also states that is expected to retain the same telephoto lens, ultra-wide sensor, LiDAR scanner, and front camera as the iPhone 17 Pro Max, suggesting the company's focus this cycle is squarely on improving the primary camera rather than overhauling the entire setup. The same leak points to 's upcoming A20 Pro chip powering the new models, built on TSMC's 2 nanometre process, along with a significantly larger battery of around 5,500mAh, which would make it the biggest battery fitted to an iPhone yet. A new colour option, referred to as Dark Cherry, and a smaller Dynamic Island have also been mentioned as part of the leaked design changes.
Since Labor Day falls on September 7 this year, mirroring the calendar in 2015, when Apple held its keynote on September 9, the analysis points to the same date this year. Going by this pattern, pre-orders would likely open on Friday, September 11, iOS 27 would roll out on Monday, September 14, review embargoes would lift around September 15 or 16, and the phones would go on sale on Friday, September 18. Mind you, Apple has not confirmed any of these dates yet.

headline: F-bombs, starry guests and candour: What we can expect from Holly Willoughby’s YouTube comeback

F-bombs, starry guests and candour: What we can expect from Holly Willoughby’s YouTube comeback Rachel McGrath Independent Digital News and Media
Holly Willoughby is back on our screens almost three years after her This Morning exit – and this time, she’s doing things a little differently. Once the darling of ITV daytime, Willoughby has shunned traditional broadcasters and is launching her comeback on her own terms, swapping mainstream media for YouTube.
The 45-year-old’s new show, Holly Willoughby Together, is being billed as a single original series but sounds a lot more like five. The programme comprises of a quintet of Together strands (get ready to read that word a lot): Talk Together, “honest in-depth conversations with people who’ve been through extraordinary things”; Cook Together, where Willoughby makes her favourite recipes “or learns from the person who knows it best”; Look Good Together for fashion and beauty;Better Together, with “practical guidance from leading experts around the everyday challenges”; and Hang Out Together, where she’ll be joined by celebrity guests.
If it sounds familiar, then that’s because it is. Together’s many pillars certainly seem Meghan Markle-esque, and simultaneously like a glossier, less tabloidy version of This Morning. And the show’s sleek, purpose-built, home-style set certainly evokes both too.
But there’s a bigger motive for the star. Willoughby’s exit from daytime came after a tumultuous period for This Morning, as her final months on the show were overshadowed when her former BFF Phillip Schofield was sacked in June 2023, after he admitted to having a relationship with a much younger colleague while he was still married.
Willoughby distanced herself from Schofield as the controversy unfolded, revealing he had denied the affair when she had previously confronted him in private. As she presented the first episode of This Morningsince the story made the headlines, she opened the show with her gravely serious yet instantly memeable “Firstly, are you OK?” monologue.
The presenter then reached her tipping point in October of the same year, quitting the show days after a man was charged over a plot to kidnap, rape and murder her. In July 2024, he was jailed for life with a minimum term of 16 years.
Addressing the terrifying case for the first time, Willoughby this week told Vogue UK: “When something like that happens, suddenly everything else gets put into perspective and, you know what? I don’t fear what people think because I know what real fear feels like.”
“Not everybody’s going to like what you do, that’s just a fact,” she continued. “I’m not for everybody. On this new platform, people find you and come to you because they’re interested in you. I’m not being forced upon anyone.”
So, will it all work? The upside, or downside, of YouTube’s immediately available viewing figures means it won’t take long to find out.
Read More
Holly Willoughby makes move to YouTube three years after This Morning exit
How to watch the World Cup in the US without YouTube TV
What is smouldering myeloma? Lauren Laverne diagnosed with rare blood disorder
Two episodes of Together will arrive each week, with the first dropping on Tuesday 28 July. A teaser trailer released today (21 July) sees Willoughby lean into her #relatable side, ditching her semi-formal This Morningwardrobe in favour of jeans, blouses and ballet pumps, referencing OnlyFans and dropping the F-word.
Perhaps having learned a vital lesson from the former Duchess of Sussex’s Netflix series With Love, Meghan, Willoughby said ahead of Together’s launch that she had to “unlearn all the telly stuff” and be more “normal” on screen. Fingers crossed she’ll manage what Meghan didn’t, and strike a relatable tone.
Together is being produced in partnership with Hungry Bear Media, which is run by Willoughby’s TV executive husband, Dan Baldwin. Numbers-wise, the move to digital makes sense. In January, analysis revealed YouTube had overtaken both ITV and the BBC on audience reach. Willoughby has already built a substantial following online, with 7.9 million Instagram followers – easily eclipsing This Morning’s 2.9 million and ITV’s dismal 800,000. She’s already had some success flying solo in the digital world too, having taken a leaf out of Gwyneth Paltrow’s book by starting a Goop-style lifestyle brand, Wylde Moon, in 2021.

Hayling Island hero lives up to 'never-give-up' motto as he gears up for triathlon challenge National World plc
A Hayland Island resident has been saluted as “superhuman” as he prepares for a new milestone in his inspirational recovery from a catastrophic brain injury.
Andy Read will don a brunette wig and specially awarded golden cape when he dresses up as Marvel icon Thor to take part in the Superhero Tri, a triathlon where everyone appears as superheroes.
It is particularly fitting that Andy will don a superhero outfit because he has won widespread admiration for his awesome powers of recovery after cheating death when he was involved in a serious car accident.
That incident, when the car he was a passenger in careered into a lamppost, left him with multiple life-changing injuries, including a severe traumatic brain injury at the age of just 20.
After fighting for his life after being airlifted to hospital, Andy was unable to walk, drink, eat or talk but he has stunned medical experts with his near miraculous recovery.
"The atmosphere is amazing and I feel that part of a community that is cheering me on to the finish line. It is a truly special event."
As he gets ready for the August 15 event - officially titled ‘Superhero Tri, powered by Marvel,’ - at Dorney Lake, Windsor, Andy has won praise from his legal team at Enable Law.
Enable Law Court of Protection Operations Lead Shannon McCullough, who is based at the law firm's Plymouth office, said: “We’re extremely proud to represent Andy because he’s such an infectiously inspirational character who is determined to live life to the full.
“His life was turned upside down, but he has approached every challenge with a positive mindset, guided by his ‘never give up, never back down,’ mantra and he is constantly striving to go further than expected."
Shannon praised Hampshire-based case manager Karen Jeffreys, of Meridian Case Management Services, for “playing a phenomenal role” in making sure Andy’s overall needs are met and the physiotherapy team at Hobbs Rehabilitation for easing him along the road to physical recovery.
Shannon added: “Andy’s a very outgoing, sociable person and every time we meet, he’s always smiling and always happy and keen to tell us his goals so he’s wonderful to work with.
“It’s been our role to work with Andy, his family, his case manager and the Hobbs Rehabilitation team to make sure everything is in place financially for his long-term future and personal ambitions like taking part in the Superhero Tri event.
"It's been amazing to see him relish every challenge like a real-life superhuman. Five years ago, Andy was only able to complete the short course, but with the support and determination around him, he is now set to complete the entire course. There's just no stopping him."
Jenny Hatfield, from Hobbs Rehabilitation, will get the triathlon under way for Andy’s team by completing the swim section in Dorney Lake. Then she will hand over to Andy and his father, Kevin, for the cycling section and they will then be joined by Andy’s brother, James, for a 10km run that will round off the challenge.
The Superhero Series is the UK’s only mass‑participation sports event designed specifically for people with disabilities, offering pressure‑free, inclusive challenges that enable everyone to unleash their superpower.
Enable Law is a corporate friend of the Superhero Series, alongside iconic brands such as Virgin Atlantic, AIG, Goldman Sachs and Oracle.
Annabelle Vaughan, the Southampton-based Head of Mental Capacity at Enable Law, said: “We are honoured to represent Andy and very proud to support the Superhero Series as corporate friends because we share its values of inclusion and empowerment.
“The Superhero Tri is a phenomenal event and a fitting stage for resilient people like Andy to show how, with the appropriate support and a positive mindset, you can bounce back from the worst misfortunes life can throw at you.”
For details about the Superhero Triathlon, email hello@superheroseries.co.uk.
Now 34-year-old Andy is able to walk with a frame, eat and drink on his own and speak digitally thanks to text-to-speech iPad software.
Andy says he is looking forward to embarking on his fifth Superhero Tri, in line with a powerful personal motto that is tattooed on his right arm.
And he will receive the 'Golden Cape Award' from the organisers in recognition of his impressive efforts.
"They said it was unlikely that I would be able to walk or move around after the accident," Andy said.
"But now I can take part in the Superhero Tri like my motto, 'never give up, never back down'.
"Superhero Tri has given me the determination to do more exercise and keep physically fit and strong and do better each year.

Matched:

|Also matched:

Source: Pakistan Law Reporter
